@@51293119 <h> Male squirrels live longer , reproduce more if they leave home : U of A study <p> EDMONTON --New research has revealed that when it comes to squirrels , it 's best for males to move away from home . <p> The study , conducted by University of Alberta ecologists , used 30 years of data on a population of North American red squirrels in Yukon . <p> It examined how the number of offspring and total lifespan differed between squirrels who lived in the same area in which they were born and those who were newcomers to the area . <p> The results showed that sex played a major role . <p> " Males benefit from moving away , whereas females do not , " said April Martinig , lead author on the study . " We also found that the decision to move away or stay at home has an impact on offspring . " <p> Moving away also meant male squirrels do n't have to compete with their siblings for mates or food . <p> For female squirrels leaving home is n't as welcoming -- they lose out on the support of nearby family , something that male squirrels do n't receive . <p> " Squirrels live in a world where there are only so many empty apartments to live in , " said Martinig . <p> " Sometimes one sibling is allowed to stay at home , so everyone else must go . If there are no vacancies nearby , squirrels then have no choice but to move further away . This is what females face , losing the benefits of having family nearby . " <p> The study also may shed light on how climate change will impact the movement of squirrels . <p> " Movement is a crucial component of species persistence , " said Martinig . " Understanding how and why certain individuals move is key to protecting populations as climate change impacts their distribution on the landscape . "

@@51293316 <p> In the United States , coal , that supervillain of fossil-fuels , is in a death spiral . But on a global scale , there 's no spiral , just an arrow pointing to Asia . The world burns 65 percent more coal today than it did in 2000 , according to the IEA 's new report . Coal accounts for 40 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions . <p> The report shows that natural gas and renewables are killing so many coal plants in the United States and Europe that worldwide coal consumption should be falling ... if it were n't for China and India . There , as well as in smaller Asian countries , coal use is rising fast enough to erase the effect of closures elsewhere . <p> IEA <p> Keisuke Sadamori , director of energy markets and security at the IEA , said that " the end of coal was heralded " when coal use shrank for three years straight in the late 1990s . " Then , between 1999 and 2013 , it grew more than it had in the preceding 90 years . " <p> That drove up pollution of carbon and the particulates that have famously choked cities like Delhi and Jakarta . It also fueled economic growth , lifting people out of poverty and helping countries prepare for the disasters made worse by climate change . For instance , despite and increase in cyclones , Bangladesh has dramatically reduced cyclone-related deaths by building shelters , fostering the growth of coastal forests , and developing systems for evacuation and cleanup . <p> There was some hope that developing countries would " leapfrog " coal and move straight to cleaner sources of energy , in the same way that some countries have skipped past landlines and adopted mobile phones . And while every country is building gas plants , solar panels , and wind turbines , most have decided that coal makes sense , too . India , for instance , is on course to increase its solar power six-fold by 2024 . But India would need much more sun-power than that to reduce its burgeoning coal consumption . <p> IEA <p> Just as Europe and the United States relied on coal to turn on electric lights in the late 19th Century , countries like China , India , Indonesia , Pakistan , and the Philippines are now doing the same . The average person in these countries still uses much less electricity than the average American . But because half the world 's population lives in this region , it 's taken a lot of coal to provide a modicum of reliable power . <p> Going forward , IEA projections show coal leveling off -- still growing but not as quickly . <p> IEA <p> These projections are based on the policies already in place , so it could all change if countries opt for other energy sources . @@51293323 <h> Alberta lawyers argue federal carbon tax unconstitutional <p> The federal carbon tax could set precedent that will erode provincial powers and should be ruled unconstitutional , lawyers for the Alberta government argued in court Monday . <p> " Prime Minister Trudeau 's carbon tax effectively amends the Constitution by expanding the power of the federal government to dictate policy in areas the Constitution says is to be regulated by the provinces , like the regulation of companies and activities that produce greenhouse gases , " said Doug Schweitzer , Alberta 's minister of justice and solicitor general , in a media release . <p> A hearing about the constitutionality of the tax is before a five-judge panel this week at the Alberta Court of Appeal in Edmonton . Alberta 's is the third provincial government to challenge the carbon tax in the legal system , after Ontario and Saskatchewan lost cases at their top provincial courts . Both have appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada . <p> Meanwhile , the justice ministers of Ontario , New Brunswick , Saskatchewan and British Columbia are all set to appear during the three days of hearings this week . <p> The carbon tax is set to take effect on Jan. 1 . The federal government , through its Pan-Canadian Framework on Clean Growth and Climate Change , requires that carbon pricing across Canada begin at $10 per tonne in 2019 and increase incrementally to $50 per tonne in 2022 . Provinces were given the freedom to develop their own plans for carbon pricing or to be subject to a mandatory federal carbon tax , often called the " carbon backstop . " <p> Speaking in court , federal lawyers cited the peace , order and good government clause -- section 91 of the Constitution Act -- in support of the carbon-tax legislation , arguing that climate change is a matter of national concern that can only effectively be addressed at the federal level . <p> Peter Gall , a lawyer representing Alberta , told the court that this was a dangerous argument . " You can call anything a national concern , " he said , arguing that federal legislation on the issue is in fact " invasive in terms of taking away policy options that would otherwise be open to the provinces . " <p> " The federal scheme might fit nicely in other provinces , but it does n't fit nicely here , " added Gall . " Regardless of what you think about the merits of its policy , the constitutionality of this legislation does not turn on the precise impact today on any particular industry , it turns on whether the federal government has the power to dictate , to impose this type of scheme . " <p> Earlier this year , Alberta 's United Conservative government passed its own plan to put a $30-per-tonne tax on greenhouse-gas emissions from large industrial emitters , including oilsands companies . The province 's environment minister Jason Nixon has said Alberta believes the policy will meet the federal government 's requirements for carbon pricing . <p> However , while federal environment minister Jonathan Wilkinson has said the Alberta plan will meet requirements for large emitters , consumers in the province may still be subject to the backstop through purchases of gas , propane and natural gas . <p> " We are committed to reducing emissions here in Alberta , but in a way that strikes the best balance for our province between environmental concerns and economic activity , " said Schweitzer . " Even if you support a carbon tax , it does n't mean that the federal government 's carbon tax is the best or only approach for every province . It is up to us to decide what works for us ; it 's not the business of Ottawa to tell us what is best for us . " <p> Later in the week , several First Nations groups , non-governmental groups and Crown corporations will speak before the court as intervenors . One of those groups , the David Suzuki Foundation , said Alberta 's industrial-emitters tax is n't robust enough to tackle climate change . <p> " There 's no more time for political stunts or delay ; we are in the midst of a climate emergency that threatens our children 's future and our rights to life , liberty and freedom , " said Suzuki Foundation science and policy director Ian Bruce in a media release . " Since the Alberta government is doing nowhere near enough to help solve the crisis , we 're forced to go to court . " <p> Bruce said a national carbon-pricing scheme is needed to effectively address climate change .

@@51293644 <p> The new partnership of residents who live year-round on the islands in the Great Lakes , called the Great Lakes Islands Alliance ( GLIA ) , held its third annual Summit on Mackinac Island in Lake Michigan in October . <p> As with previous gatherings , participants reminded themselves that the Great Lakes hold about 20 per cent of the world 's fresh water and living on islands comes with the responsibility of protecting the integrity of this critical resource . <p> Participants have come to visualize the five Great Lakes as gently sloping eastward from the west coast of Lake Superior to the east coast of Lake Ontario , and as a result , Great Lakes waters eventually flow into the St. Lawrence River and the Atlantic Ocean . <p> Of concern to island residents is that this eastward flow means that pollution in the waters of Thunder Bay and Duluth , for example , will eventually make its way around and past all the Great Lakes islands to the east . Likewise , pollution from the islands , along with that of cities on the shoreline such as Milwaukie , Sault Ste. Marie , and Cleveland , ends up flowing around islands to the east . <p> Of all the topics discussed at the three annual summits , environmental issues were the most prominent . Impacts of climatic change , loss of forests and biodiversity , and invasive species were all of concern , but issues relating to water quality were particularly highlighted . <p> Sudbury is not on the shores of a Great Lake , but it is in the Great Lakes watershed , so I decided to research the various forms of polluted wastewaters that are discharged from the Sudbury region and the route they take as they flow away from our region . <p> The City of Greater Sudbury encompasses a large and mostly rural area of 33,637 square kilometres containing 330 lakes and associated streams and rivers . In all , Sudbury embraces a greater number and larger diversity of lakes than any other city in Canada . Many of these lakes historically provided essential services such as drinking water and effluent disposal . <p> Unfortunately , a long history of industrial pollution , inadequate sewage disposal systems , urban runoff and lakeshore development has seriously degraded the water quality of many of these lakes . About 7,000 lakes within a 17,000-square-km area encompassing the City of Greater Sudbury were acidified to pH 6.0 or below by the 1980s . Damage to aquatic organisms occurs at this level of acidification . <p> History of Sudbury 's impact on aquatic ecosystems <p> Sudbury was established in 1882 near a railway junction spanning the now aptly-named Junction Creek.Unlike most cities in Canada , Sudbury was not built on a navigable river or lake , but at some distance inland to mine and process rich deposits of nickel and copper . <p> The extractive economy was not kind to local ecosystems . Indeed , mining and smelting so badly damaged the local environment that the Sudbury Basin became one of the most heavily contaminated regions on the planet . <p> Copper Cliff Creek with tailings effluent near the Copper Cliff Public School . This water has exited the tailings pond area and is flowing towards a Vale treatment plant prior to being discharged into Junction Creek . Joe Shorthouse photo.jpg , SU <p> Open roast beds used for smelting ores before to the 1920s added S02 and particles of copper , nickel and other metals into the air , which settled on the hills and lakes and destroyed vegetation . With the vegetation destroyed on hilltops , exposed acidic soil with elevated metals washed into depressions and nearby lakes and creeks . <p> It is estimated that more than 100 million tons of S02 and thousands of tons of metal particles were deposited in the Sudbury area . At the same time , clear-cut logging to obtain wood for the roast beds led to the destruction of nearly 20,000 ha of land and about 80,000 ha of the landscape became barren . <p> One of the most damaged aquatic ecosystems in the Sudbury area was Junction Creek . This creek , about 50 km in length , stretches through the Greater Sudbury , from Garson to the southwest of Sudbury , before emptying into Kelly Lake . Junction Creek was used by early Sudburians as a source of drinking water , but also a place downstream to dispose of domestic sewage . Pollutants carried by water from the Inco complex ( now known as Vale ) also flowed into Junction Creek . <p> Sawmills were built on several Sudbury lakes and streams including Minnow Lake , Ramsey Lake and Junction Creek . The mill on Minnow Lake operated for 23 years and during this period sawdust and wood waste were dumped into the lake . <p> A creosote plant ( a toxic chemical used to treat railroad ties ) on Lorne Street added pollutants from the 1920s to 1960 , as did untold other industries . <p> Waters of Junction Creek flow into Kelly Lake to the southwest of Sudbury and it quickly became one of the most polluted lakes in the country . So much soil contaminated with acid , heavy metals , debris and sewage entered the lake that a huge alluvial fan of deposits developed at the entry point . <p> The city initially relied on water currents to disperse the sewage dumped into Junction Creek , but as the population grew in the 1930s and 1940s , the need arose for proper sewers and sewage treatment plants . Establishing a flow of sewage to treatment facilities was difficult in Sudbury because of the rocky and rolling topography necessitating many lift stations . <p> The solution was the construction of a series of rock tunnels starting in 1962 to bring the sewage to the southwest part of the city near Kelly Lake Road . The rock tunnel is about 1.5 metres wide and 2.1 metres high and now is more than 21 km long , making Sudbury the only city in Canada with such a sewage system . <p> Pumps brought the untreated sewage to the surface where it was discharged intoJunction Creek and Kelly Lake , and it either settled to the bottom or was washed away to the southwest . <p> Dumping raw sewage into a creek and lake was clearly unsuitable . By 1972 , the first sewage treatment plant was in operation and then over the years , eight more municipal sewage treatment plants and three sewage lagoons were constructed , all operated by various municipalities . In addition , there are two wastewater treatment plants built by the mining companies . Four of the treatment plants release their waters into the Vermillion River watershed west of Sudbury , as does the mining complex in Copper Cliff . <p> Sewage lagoons consist of settling ponds where solids are broken down and then the waters are released into a creek or river . Sewage treatment plants in Garson and Falconbridge east of Sudbury release their waters into the Wanapitei watershed , which also eventually enters Lake Huron . <p> Waters of Junction Creek flow into Kelly Lake to the southwest of Sudbury and it quickly became one of the most polluted lakes in the country . So much soil contaminated with acid , heavy metals , debris and sewage entered the lake that a huge alluvial fan of deposits developed at the entry point . <p> Mike Jensen of the City of Greater Sudbury recently gave me a tour of the Kelly Lake plant . The tour started with a trip to the base of the shaft where huge pumps push the sewage to the surface . <p> Waste that enters the highly efficient , automated and almost odour-free plant contains our body wastes , and water used in bathing , clothes and dishwashing . Once on the surface , non-decomposable items such as diapers , wipes , and sanitary napkins -- none of which should ever be flushed down a toilet -- are first removed by a series of bar screens . <p> The water then enters four aeration tanks where bubbles churn the liquid , which helps bacteria breakdown solids . There are also six circular clarifier tanks where solids ( now called sludge ) settles to the bottom and then is turned into an environmentally-friendly biosolid , which is used for soil enrichment for farms and industrial land reclamation . <p> After the bacterial breakdown of solids and clarification , chlorine is added to the treated water to kill bacteria such as E. coli . The wastewater , which is now clear , is then discharged into Junction Creek . <p> One continuing issue for Sudbury 's wastewater treatment system it that its sewers were designed to carry both sewage ( waters from toilets , sinks and drains ) and stormwater ( rain or snowmelt ) . Such combined sewers were cheaper to install at the outset , but their flaw occurs when heavy rainfall and rapid snowmelt overwhelm the sewage treatment plant 's capacity , whereupon sewage is dosed with chlorine but otherwise untreated , and allowed to bypass the plant and flow directly into Junction Creek . <p> This problem is so serious that during periods of high flows , as much as 400 million litres per day are received rather than 65 , million litres for which the plant was designed . Known as either a bypass or overcapacity , this happened 47 times at the Kelly Lake Plant in 2018 . <p> Waste Water from the Vale Complex west of Sudbury <p> The two large mining and smelting companies in Greater Sudbury ( Inco , now Vale in Copper Cliff and Falconbridge , now Glencore in Falconbridge ) were historically responsible for most of the pollution and environmental damage in Sudbury . <p> Monitoring records indicate that sulphur dioxide emissions peaked at 5,600 tonnes per day from 1960 to 1975 , as did lake acidification . Both companies once dumped untreated wastewater from their smelter complexes directly into local creeks and rivers , but of different watersheds . Waters from Inco/Vale exited the property into Junction Creek , whereas waters from Falconbridge/Glencore entered enter into the Wanapitei River , which drains into the French River . <p> Both companies use vast amounts of water in the processing of their ores . Most water is used to move and deposit tailings , the waste rock remaining after crushing the ore and removing the valuable minerals . Mining industries in Sudbury produce about 10 million tons of tailings each year and store them on their property . <p> Vale 's tailings are deposited in depressions to the west of Copper Cliff . Water that settles to the base of the tailings ponds is returned to the crushing complex and reused , but some escapes and flows into creeks on company property . <p> Most of the water that exits the tailings is treated by the company and then is released into Copper Cliff Creek , which joins Junction Creek . Not all the acidity and metals are removed from the wastewater , but the company must meet regulatory limits for pH , metals and ammonia and the water they discharge must also pass toxicity tests to certain aquatic organisms . <p> Vale 's tailings are dark gray when they arrive at the disposal site , but turn orange when they dry out and generate acid . To the company 's credit , and the pioneering work of the late Tom Peters , forest ecosystems have been developed on the surface of older tailings which seal in the acidic components . The company currently uses municipal biosolids to help establish a robust vegetative cover on the surface of the tailings , which helps limit water infiltration and increase biodiversity . <p> 1221 su accent Map.SU.jpgjpg , SU <p> Another waste by-product from the smelting process is slag.Slag is the waste material from the smelter after the metals are liquefied and extracted at high temperatures from crushed ore and then deposited in slag heaps . Vale 's slag storage area has been in use since 1929 and contains more than 115 million tonnes of smelter waste . <p> Waters washing off slag heaps are contaminated and some runoff makes its way into local creeks . For example , in 2012 , elevated levels of metals and acidity were found in Nolin 's Creek which exits a slag heap in west Sudbury . <p> Throughout the history of Inco/Vale , a huge slag heap slowly formed on the western edge of Sudbury . Thanks to the pioneering work of Vale 's Environment Department , vegetation has been established on the surface . So many flowers appear each year that beehives have been installed and monarch butterflies feed on milkweed . <p> Route of water from Sudbury to Lake Huron <p> Using Google Maps , the flow of waste and treated waters can be followed southwestward from Sudbury and southeastward from Falconbridge into Lake Huron . The route southwestward is more complex and is the only one followed here . <p> Junction Creek flows into Kelly Lake where debris , sediment and pollutants throughout the history of Sudbury have built up in a huge deposit , which is clearly visible in Google Maps . From Kelly Lake , Junction Creek continues southwest and enters Mud Lake . Waters from the west end of Vale 's tailings complex also flow into Mud Lake . <p> From Mud Lake , the waters flow into Simon Lake and then McCharles Lake , where the waters join the Vermilion River . The Vermilion River at this point already has received treated wastewaters from communities north of Sudbury , as well as treated effluent from Vale and Glencore which enters Onaping River , a tributary of the Vermilion . <p> The Vermillion River then enters Rat , Grassy , Ella and Wabagishik lakes , and thereafter joins the Spanish River south of the Highway 17 crossing . <p> After its confluence with the Vermilion River , the Spanish River flows past the town of Espanola where it receives treated wastewaters from the town and the Domtar pulp mill . Downstream from Espanola , the Spanish River flows westward past the towns of Webbwood and Massey , then enters Lake Huron near the town of Spanish . <p> Once in Lake Huron , Sudbury 's effluent and the effluent from downstream sources enters the North Channel -- the body of water between the mainland and Manitoulin Island . At its widest point , the North Channel is about 30 km wide and is recognized as the best freshwater boating area in the world . <p> The waters then flow eastward past Green , Aird , Eagle , Frechette , Fox , Amedroz and Bedford Islands in the North Channel before passing through the two channels north and south of Goat Island.At Goat Island , the south channel passes under the swing bridge at Little Current . <p> This means that when a toilet is flushed in Sudbury , the wastewater ultimately flows down the North Channel past the Manitoulin Island community of Little Current and the swing bridge . <p> Polluted sediments at the mouth of the Spanish River <p> The Vermillion and Spanish Rivers historically have been affected along their entire length by the cumulative impacts of logging , untreated and treated domestic waste , and a legacy of mining contaminants.Most contaminants were washed along the river bed , but some accumulated in areas with little current . <p> Today , a citizen group called the Vermilion River Stewardship acts as a voice for the Vermilion River and strives to preserve and protect its natural beauty and health . They monitor and draw attention to changes in water quality . <p> In 1994 , a group of concerned citizens , including some who lived along the shores of the Spanish River downstream from Espanola established the Friends of the Spanish River , which was dedicated to " restoring , preserving , and celebrating " the river by insisting measures be taken to prevent further pollution . <p> While the levels of heavy metals in the Vermillion and Spanish rivers have dramatically decreased thanks to reduced input from mining , large amounts of toxic metals are still buried at the mouth of the Spanish River under deposits of contaminated soil from the hills of Sudbury . <p> This citizen action group came about partially in response to a spill of 180,000 litres of sodium or potassium salt from the Espanola mill in 1983 that killed fish from Espanola to the mouth of the Spanish River . The volunteers were so successful in helping the river return to health that sport fish are able again to thrive . The group was disbanded after 19 years having achieved its mission . <p> While the levels of heavy metals in the Vermillion and Spanish rivers have dramatically decreased thanks to reduced input from mining , large amounts of toxic metals are still buried at the mouth of the Spanish River under deposits of contaminated soil from the hills of Sudbury . <p> As a result , the Spanish Harbour is deemed an ' Area of Concern In Recovery ' by the International Joint Commission ( IJC ) . The IJC is a bi-national organization established by the governments of Canada and the United States to prevent and resolve disputes about the use and quality of boundary waters . <p> A 2018 report by aquatic scientists found that contaminant levels in the Spanish River and Spanish Harbour , along with levels in waters in the North Channel , have shown a steady decline . Pollutants in the Spanish harbour are currently being encased by non-polluted sediments such that it is thought best not to attempt removing the contaminated sediments by dredging . <p> Sudbury a model for ecosystem rehabilitation <p> After a century of exposure to high levels of pollutants , and the discomfort of living in a city with a negative image , citizens of Sudbury in the early 1970s started demanding that harmful levels of emissions from the smelters be reduced . After much hard work and commitment , ways were found to return vegetation to the black , acid-washed hillsides of their city . <p> Government regulations resulted in major reductions in toxic emissions from the three Sudbury smelters . One smelter was closed , while technological and process changes were made to the INCO/Vale and Falconbridge/Glencore smelters resulting in dramatic decreases in sulphur dioxide emissions . <p> Pioneering research in the mid-1970s by Prof. Keith Winterhalder of Laurentian University showed that when just the right amount of crushed limestone and fertilizer is applied to bare rock , along with seeds of plants tolerant to harsh conditions , green grass takes hold the following year . <p> Using this new technique , it was discovered that once grasses were established , seeds of other plants blew in from elsewhere and green terrestrial ecosystems began to appear . White birch was the first tree species to become established . Thereafter , Sudbury initiated a program of planting trees , which continues to this day . <p> Dr. Joe Shorthouse is a retired professor of entomology and environmental biology at Laurentian University in Sudbury and is a member of the Steering Committee of the Great Lakes Islands Alliance . Here he is standing at the underground exit of the Sudbury sewage tunnel beside one of four 525 hp pumps each capable of moving 80 , 000 , 000 litres of wastewater per day . Mike Jensen of the City of Greater Sudbury.jpg , SU <p> Where highways leading into Sudbury were lined with blackened , acid-washed rock in 1975 , today healthy coniferous forests grow to welcome visitors . More than 10 million trees have been planted to date . Restoration activities by the mining companies and the City of Greater Sudbury have been coordinated since 1973 by a committee called the Vegetation Enhancement Technical Advisory Committee , or VETAC . Sudbury 's success at restoration has received international attention and many awards . <p> Reductions in pollutant emissions , revegetation and reforestation of barren hillsides have resulted in improvements in water quality and recoveries of fish communities . However , the hillsides around Sudbury still contain enough metals to sustain high levels in some lakes and rainfall still causes the release of previously deposited pollutants from the catchment . The remarkable improvements made so far show that further remediation efforts are likely to improve conditions even more . <p> Even Junction Creek has been dramatically improved . A citizen group called the Junction Creek Stewardship Committee monitors the health of the creek each summer and aides in restoring it to a natural functioning ecosystem . While the creek still suffers from multiple stressors such as municipal wastewater discharge and stormwater runoff with high levels of salt and phosphorus , the waters are clean enough that brook trout can be stocked in the creek each spring . <p> Final comments <p> Those of us who live in Greater Sudbury should understand and remember that our city is part of a larger Great Lakes ecosystem . Our wastewater flows all the way to the North Channel of Manitoulin Island , and beyond . As the stewards of a region <p> with extensive extractive industry , we have the responsibility of making sure Sudbury 's wastewater is as free of pollutants as possible before allowing it to pass into the Great Lakes . <p> Consider also that our waste , although diluted , passes by drinking water intake pipes for the Manitoulin communities of Gore Bay , Kagawong , and Little Current.Once the wastewater passes the east shore of Manitoulin Island , it flows down the east coast of Lake Huron , through Lake Erie , over Niagara Falls , then past Montreal and Quebec City on its way to the Atlantic Ocean . <p> Sudburians are justifiably proud that through timely and concerted efforts by its citizens , governments , and scientists , our aquatic ecosystems have shown impressive recovery in the past 30 years . This recovery has been monitored by scientists with the Living With Lakes Centre on the campus of Laurentian University , and their results have illustrated that aquatic improvement is directly correlated with reductions in industrial emissions . Their studies of the improvements provide some of the best evidence in the world supporting the implementation of pollution control programs . <p> The progress made so far in restoring Sudbury 's aquatic ecosystems is both remarkable and encouraging , but the problem is by no means solved and will remain with us for the foreseeable future . Today , we should be taking steps to ensure that no untreated wastewaters from mine tailings enter aquatic ecosystems . <p> The progress made so far in restoring Sudbury 's aquatic ecosystems is both remarkable and encouraging , but the problem is by no means solved and will remain with us for the foreseeable future . Today , we should be taking steps to ensure that no untreated wastewaters from mine tailings enter aquatic ecosystems . <p> Similarly , the number of overflows of raw sewage into Junction Creek that occur each year remains a serious issue . As Sudbury prepares for climate change , its residents should make a concerted effort to ensure that their rooftop runoff and other stormwater controls exit into ditches or onto lawns , so that stormwater is not added to the domestic sewage system . <p> In addition to policy changes , there is much we can do at a personal level to fulfill our stewardship obligations . We can avoid dumping toxic and biologically harmful substances into our wastewater systems that flow into Lake Huron . We can avoid using excessive fertilizer , insecticide and herbicide on our soils , where they will be carried by rain into groundwater and riparian systems . <p> We must all understand that harmful and toxic substances come in many unexpected forms . For example , unused medication and household cleaning fluids should never be flushed down toilets . Studies have shown that a sufficient amount of pharmaceuticals make their way into aquatic food webs that male fish downstream from release sites have smaller testes , and male fish are turned into females . <p> As discussed above , the extractive industry historically has had an outsized impact on the health of Sudbury 's aquatic systems . Over time , however , it has become clear that the effects of large and small scale industry on environmental health can be brought under control through policy change and citizen action.While this is so , the problem is bigger than industry alone . We must also individually be vigilant in how we treat the waters in our care . <p> -- Dr. Joe Shorthouse is a retired professor of entomology and environmental biology at Laurentian University in Sudbury , Ontario and is a member of the Steering Committee of the Great Lakes Islands Alliance .

@@51293817 <p> As forestry companies run out of easy-to-access timber , loggers are forced to move higher , which requires specialized steep-slope logging equipment Submitted <p> Anyone who has ever flown from Vancouver to Prince Rupert , Prince George or Fort Nelson and looked out the window may have wondered to themselves : " How can B.C. possibly be running out of trees to cut ? " <p> B.C. 's forest sector was beaten to a pulp in 2019 , as a " perfect storm " of market , policy and natural forces converged , triggering multiple sawmill closures and curtailments , and spurring anger among laid-off workers towards politicians and conservationists . <p> When the Sierra Club and Wilderness Committee tried to hold an event in Campbell River on November 25 , it was shut down by the city and police , for fear of confrontation . What was supposed to be a town hall talk on old-growth forests and climate change turned into an impromptu pro-logging rally , according to the Campbell River Mirror . <p> " It 's not a very popular time to be an environmentalist , " said Mark Worthing , a climate and conservation campaigner for the Sierra Club . <p> Nor is it a popular time to be a BC NDP cabinet minister in ridings where sawmill workers and loggers are now struggling to meet mortgage and car payments . There , the general downturn in forestry is aggravated by a prolonged strike by Western Forest Products ( TSX:WEF ) workers . When Claire Trevena , NDP MLA for North Island , held a recent town hall in Campbell River , angry , out-of-work loggers accused government of indifference to their plight . <p> B.C. forestry companies have gone from making record profits in 2017 and 2018 to posting losses in 2019 . <p> " The companies are bleeding , " John Desjardins , forest products lead for KPMG in Canada , said at a recent Greater Vancouver Board of Trade talk on forestry . " They 're in the red . " <p> Six sawmills permanently closed in 2019 , and with shifts that have been eliminated at mills that are still operating , it adds up to the equivalent of eight sawmills . <p> Thousands of sawmill workers , truck loggers and related service workers were laid off in 2019 . Employment and Social Development Canada confirms that unemployment insurance claims went up in B.C. by 1,170 between September 2018 and the same month in 2019 . <p> The effects are most immediately felt in Interior towns like 100 Mile House , where forestry accounts for one out of every four jobs . But forestry accounts for one-third of B.C. 's exports , and even in Vancouver , the economic impact will be felt , because more sawmill closures are inevitable -- possibly followed by pulp mill closures . <p> " More than 40% of forestry jobs are located in Vancouver and in the southwest part of the province , " Susan Yurkovich , CEO of the BC Council of Forest Industries , recently told the Greater Vancouver Board of Trade , adding that forestry in B.C. accounts for 100,000 direct and indirect jobs . <p> Forestry is cyclical , and B.C. is used to downturns . " This time it 's different , " Yurkovich said . <p> Other provinces , like Quebec , have not seen the wave of sawmill closures that B.C. has . Whereas B.C. used to be " the last man standing " when a cyclical downturn came in forestry -- owing to the fact it was a low-cost jurisdiction -- that 's no longer the case . <p> One of the biggest problems has become a lack of economically harvestable timber . In a province with 55 million hectares of forest -- an area roughly three times the size of the U.K. -- how is that possible ? <p> The most visible answer is the toll taken by the mountain pine beetle , and by forest fires . But it 's not just pests and natural disasters that have eaten up B.C. 's timber supply . Pressure to preserve forests for conservation or yield them to recreation and increased urbanization have resulted in a significant shrinkage of the working-forest land base . <p> " We need to invest in and protect the working-forest land base , " Yurkovich said . " We should decide on the size of the working-forest land base , and then we should lock it in . " <p> She added that the industry is burdened by a " jungle " of regulations that increase operating costs . <p> But drawing a moat around B.C. 's working forests is easier said than done . For one thing , it 's not likely to win the support of conservation groups , which continue to press for less logging , not more . <p> " I can see what Yurkovich might be gunning for there , " the Sierra Club 's Worthing said . " We 'd never particularly stand behind super checkerboard , black-and-white sacrifice zones and conservation zones that have discrete lines in that way , because that 's not really how ecosystems work . <p> " I would say that the timber-harvesting land base has n't been chewed away at by other interests . It 's been really heavily logged on really short rotations . And I would argue that the large tenure holders and the major logging corporations have basically run through a resource far too fast and have not been managing their existing timber-harvesting land base sustainably . " <p> On paper , B.C. should theoretically still have sufficient working forests to supply mills . In reality , some of the timber deemed working forest is too costly under the current system to log . <p> Jim Girvan , an independent forestry consultant , points to the Prince George timber supply area ( TSA ) as an example . At eight million hectares , it is the single largest TSA in B.C. <p> But once all the exclusions for recreation , wildlife habitat conservation , old-growth preservation and other measures are accounted for , it leaves just three million hectares that can be logged , Girvan said . <p> " They identify the land base on paper , but it 's not a circle on a map because you still have landscape restrictions , " Girvan said . <p> The allowable annual cut in B.C. is nominally bigger than what is harvested . BC Government <p> If the Prince George TSA is further apportioned as First Nations tenures , as has been proposed , it would reduce the allowable annual cut ( AAC ) a further 3% to 4% , Girvan said . <p> " There 's another shift gone , just because you 're drawing different lines on a map , " Girvan said . <p> The coastal cut has shrunk by 8.5 million cubic metres since the 1990s . That is enough to supply 10 coastal sawmills , Girvan said . The Great Bear Rainforest alone took 6.4 million hectares . Only 295,000 hectares were preserved for logging . <p> " In that 295,000 hectares , now you 're very restricted on what you can log . " <p> Increased log exports have been blamed , in part , for the shortage of timber on the B.C. coast -- something the NDP government has been trying to address with new regulations . Girvan does n't think any of the regulations that the government has adopted will address the fundamental problem of access to timber . <p> " It 's not log exports -- it 's because the cut went down , " Girvan said . " The cut 's going down because they 're systematically preserving more and more timber for a variety of reasons . " <p> The long-term annual allowable cut will continue to decline , especially in the interior . <p> While he agrees that declaring working-forest boundaries with regulatory goalposts that do n't move would go a long way to ensuring the long-term viability of forestry in B.C. , Girvan said the pressure from urban development is unrelenting . <p> He cites controversy over a plan to log in the Mount Elphinstone area of the Sunshine Coast as an example . <p> Despite having set aside 15,400 hectares for parks and conservation , and 2,900 hectares of old growth , the province is under continued pressure to stop logging in the area that is still designated for harvesting . It has reduced the logging area on the south slope to just 27 hectares per year -- half of what the AAC for that area would support . <p> And just recently , the B.C. government called a halt to all logging in the Skagit River valley in an exclusion zone between Manning and Skagit provincial parks called the " doughnut hole . " <p> " The problem with putting a circle on a map and saying ' This is logging ' is that it never gains traction because of this growing urban interface , " Girvan said . " Eventually somebody will move next door to it and say , ' Oh no , no , you ca n't log in my backyard . ' " <p> While an ever-shrinking land base is part of the problem in B.C. , the cost of harvesting is also a challenge . There are stands of trees that could be cut but which simply do not provide an economic return . <p> And there are plenty of trees in the northern half of B.C. , which could be opened up to logging , but the distance and remoteness would add to the cost of harvesting and transporting logs . <p> " You could move further north , but you run into economics , " said John Innes , the dean of the faculty of forestry at the University of British Columbia . <p> He added that the working forests are not being managed in a way that maximizes the timber resource , the way they are in northern Europe . <p> " We could be growing our trees more intensively , we could be growing them faster , we could be producing a higher volume from the same area , " he said , adding that that would be a very long-term project . <p> He also points out that it is the big forestry companies in B.C. that have been hit the hardest by the lack of timber , increasing costs and falling lumber prices . <p> " It is still possible to make money with trees in British Columbia , " Innes said . " We have the big mills focusing on dimensional lumber , and those are the ones that have been suffering . But if you look at the smaller specialty mills , they generally have been doing OK still . " 
@@51295532 <p> We 've already seen the political parties and their leaders staking out positions on an array of fundamental issues . Whether it 's climate change , taxes , employment , foreign policy , immigration or health care , we have a pretty good idea where each party stands . <p> But what if we told you we do n't know what the parties ' plans are for an economic sector that employs almost 2.5 million people and directly helps millions of Canadians in every province and territory every day ? Would you believe us ? Well , it 's true . <p> I 'm referring to the social purpose sector -- charities , non-profits , and social enterprises . <p> Perhaps this policy silence is because , by and large , " charities " are not controversial . Few Canadians -- and even fewer politicians -- would argue against a sector that helps to protect our most vulnerable neighbours ; that gives us the opportunity to express our faith ; that provides opportunities for our children to participate in sports and the arts ; that funds research into critical illnesses and provides direct aid to those suffering from those illnesses ; that responds to natural disasters and international crises , and that advances the well-being of seniors . And that 's just the tip of the iceberg . <p> We know our sector is appreciated and supported . Canadians are among the most generous people in the world in terms of both financial support and volunteering . The fact that 13 million Canadians freely give their time and skills to support charitable causes speaks for itself . <p> But our world is rapidly changing . Powerful demographic and economic shifts are making it increasingly difficult for charities and non-profits to effectively respond to community needs and demands . <p> Imagine Canada 's Chief Economist for the Charitable and Non-profit Sector has crunched the numbers and identified a looming " social deficit " that 's expected to hit $25 billion a year within a decade . This means that in just a few years social purpose organizations will need $25 billion more than they have today to meet demand . <p> Quite simply , the social deficit is the difference between the demand for services social purpose organizations provide , and the resources available to deliver those services . Unlike household debt or government deficits , this deficit wo n't show up on a balance sheet . Instead , it will manifest itself in hardship caused by reduced services and longer wait times along with increased pressure on staff and volunteers to do more with less . <p> We are calling on all federal parties to recognize this challenge and commit to working with us to ensure a sustainable future where we can keep providing vital services that individuals and communities have come to rely on . <p> Government can do much to strengthen the social purpose sector . Some progress has been made in recent years by governments of all political stripes . Changes to the tax system have made it easier for Canadians to donate . The Social Finance Fund announced last year has the potential to help organizations access new and innovative sources of funding . <p> The next step is action to reform the outdated regulatory framework governing charities and non-profits . The next federal government should also give the sector a seat at the policy table . <p> Canada 's 170,000 social purpose organizations excel at inclusiveness and creating social value in areas ranging from health care to social services , education and the environment . This expertise is a largely untapped public policy resource with the potential to improve the lives of Canadians from coast-to-coast-to-coast . <p> When a candidate shows up on your doorstep , ask them what their party is going to do to support charities and non-profits . Even better , be proactive . Reach out to the candidates and explain how action to strengthen social purpose organizations will influence your voter choice . <p> Together , we can send a message that no government will be able to ignore .

Or even know what they are . <p> Adults may have their own dreams . And wishes . <p> As it turns out , we have a few . Perhaps we have a wish or two that will inspire you to make a few wishes of your own . <p> The lesson of Christmas , of course , is to never stop believing . And , in the spirit of Christmas giving , here are our top four wishes : <p> 1 . We wish for a pollinator-friendly world . Imagine if birds , bees and myriad other insects -- all responsible for pollinating more than 30 per cent of our food -- were not under threat . Come the warmer months , there is a buzz in our gardens that is as sweet as honey . Sweeter still , since this buzz is the sound of workers who never take a day off or complain about their task . They just get out there and buzz the flowers that produce the fruits and vegetables that feed us . It may be hard to imagine a threat-free life for pollinators when we so seldom think of them at all . <p> Truth is , they are easy to overlook . A mason bee is so small that you would have to bend over and concentrate to see one buzzing in your balsam . <h> YOU MIGHT BE INTERESTED IN ... <p> 2 . We wish people would stop pointing fingers . Mature people point at young people and demand they act more responsible . Young people point at boomers and ask them to change their habits ( we thank you , climate-change activist Greta Thunberg , Time 's 2019 person of the year ) . While both sides have their points , this is no way to change the world . Change starts with action . Grandparents want their grandchildren to know that they do care about the world they are handing over to the next generation . This is why many of them in the GTA will walk in the GrandTrees Walk with Nature at Evergreen Brickworks this coming Mother 's Day , May 10 , 2020 . Grandchildren ( and their parents ) are invited . <p> 3 . We wish more people would embrace rot and decay . These are not words that garden communicators of the past would use to describe a great garden or a wonderful gardening experience . But gardeners have changed . A visit this past summer to Great Dixter House &amp; Gardens , in the English village of Northiam , East Sussex , showed us a great example . One of the most popular public gardens in the Queen 's realm , Dixter features a compost pile so old , and so high , you can drive a tractor through it . <p> What 's the point ? At the foundation of every great garden is an equally great compost pile . Or some source of rich , organic material . To plant and nurture a garden without it makes less sense than growing the same crop on the same soil every year without replenishing the organic material that is drained from it each season . This is strip mine farming -- and it is neither sustainable nor smart . Rot and decay are our friends . <p> 4 . We wish for sunshine , roses , amazing sunsets and rain when needed . Of course , none of these things will occur quite when we planned . The sun will roast your potatoes mid-summer , roses in Southern Ontario are now susceptible to Japanese beetles ( thank you climate change ) , amazing sunsets will occur just infrequently enough to leave us breathless , and rain will fall on someone 's parade . <p> Get more real estate in your inbox <p> Get more stories about owning , renting , and just getting by in Toronto and beyond with our Real Estate email newsletter . <p> The fact is , nature is in control of nature . You can prove it by moving out of your house for a year and not cutting the grass , weeding the patio stones or cleaning your eavestroughs . When you return , you will see thistles for lawn , hay for a patio and trees growing in your rain gutters . That is the power of nature . <h> YOU MIGHT BE INTERESTED IN ... <p> Our Christmas wish for you is that you will find nature in ways that never occurred to you before . We believe that all of us will . And it can happen by simply putting the phone away , and sitting on the garden bench . <p> Mark and Ben Cullen are expert gardeners and contributors for the Star . @@51297400 <h> Is Wall Street Turning Its Back On Fossil Fuels ? <p> Goldman Sachs said that it would no longer finance coal projects , or oil and gas exploration in the Arctic . <p> In a new environmental policy framework , the investment bank acknowledged the urgency of climate change and noted that not acting would be " costly for our natural environment , humans and to the economy . " <p> It appears to be the first time one of the largest U.S. banks has cut off financing for entire swathes of the fossil fuel sector . " Goldman Sachs 's updated policy shows that US banks can draw red lines on oil and gas , and now other major US banks , especially JPMorgan Chase -- the world 's worst banker of fossil fuels by a wide margin -- must improve on what Goldman has done , " Jason Ope ? a Disterhoft of Rainforest Action Network said in a statement . <p> Goldman Sachs also said that it would make $750 billion in financing available for " climate transition and inclusive growth finance " over the next decade . <p> Separately , Morgan Stanley wrote in a note that the focus on ESG ( environment , social and governance issues ) has increased , " creating both risks and opportunities " for the U.S. energy sector . An " ESG discount " is not yet evident , Morgan Stanley said , but there is an " increasing risk of relative underperformance for companies that fail to integrate ESG best practices into their core business . " Going forward , the bank said , " we expect the focus on ESG to intensify . " <p> Activist investors also continue to mount pressure from within companies themselves . The Dutch shareholder activist group Follow This is preparing more climate resolutions at the upcoming annual shareholder meetings of ExxonMobil , Chevron , Royal Dutch Shell and Equinor . <p> In a major " decarbonization " report issued earlier this month , Goldman Sachs noted that the number of climate-related shareholder proposals has almost doubled since 2011 , and the percentage of shareholders voting in favor of those resolutions has tripled . Half of those resolutions target the oil , gas , utilities and coal industries . " In our view , this is creating a severe tightening of financing conditions across the hydrocarbon industry , leading to a new age of capital constraint , " the investment bank said in a report . <p> However , it is important to note that shifting financial conditions of certain industries undercuts the significance of Goldman 's new policy . The coal industry is dying a slow but painful death ; it 's not clear why major investment banks would want to get into that sector anyway . The same is true for Arctic oil . Royal Dutch Shell abandoned a major Arctic exploration program earlier this decade , and it was n't because of concerns about climate change . <p> Goldman can simply close the door on unprofitable financing ventures while also taking credit for " leading " on climate change . Notably , Goldman did not close the door on other forms of oil and gas , including oil sands and shale . <p> Furthermore , the bank notes that " underinvestment " in oil will lead to " structural " supply tightness in the 2020s . In a recent equity research note , the investment bank sees this as an opportunity , and finds companies that are " undervalued " that it can recommend to its clients . So , the commitment to sustainability only goes so far . <p> But , debt-fueled drilling has also turned some banks and lenders away from shale as well . " Reserve-based lending to E&amp;Ps for new oil &amp; gas developments is down 90% from the peak , " Goldman wrote . Tighter financial conditions in the oil and gas industry is leading to consolidation and higher barriers to entry , creating a " new oligopoly " in the oil industry . <p> " High yield credit to the US E&amp;Ps , the financing of choice of smaller US shale producers , has also dried up since the beginning of 2019 , leading to a 25% fall in US shale activity ytd . " As smaller companies are forced out , the bank says the sector 's profits could rise . <p> In its decarbonization report , Goldman urges the oil majors to undertake a transformation into lower carbon businesses . Dubbed the " Re-Imagining Big Oils " analysis , Goldman says the majors can pivot into a variety of other sectors , including EV recharging , renewables , biofuels , nature-based solutions and carbon capture . <p> " This transition will require deep cultural and corporate changes and may leave the higher carbon parts of the value chain financially stranded and underinvested , such as oil production , " the bank concluded . <p> Goldman Sachs cutting off coal and Artic oil is another milestone in the energy transition , although its immediate impact is debatable . Big Finance is still very much in the game for the rest of the fossil fuel sector . 
@@51297428 <h> Birds of a feather count together <p> Jim Thompson , Kurt Hennige and Chris Tsokos were three of the 27 volunteers out counting birds in the Napanee region for the 120th annual Christmas Bird Count on Saturday , Dec. 22 , 2019 . They spotted some ravens and waterfowl at Finkle 's Shore Park in Bath before moving on to other areas on Saturday morning . Meghan Balogh/The Whig-Standard/Postmedia Networkjpg , KI <p> Every winter , during the holiday season , dedicated ' birders ' head out into designated regions across North America , in all weather conditions , to count bird species . <p> The annual Christmas Bird Count is marking its 120th year this year , and it could be the largest , longest-running " citizen science project " ever undertaken , says Kurt Hennige . <p> Hennige is a longtime local birder who has been involved in preservation and research for much of his life , including working on loggerhead shrike projects in the Napanee area with Wildlife Preservation Canada . He 's been participating in Christmas bird counts since the 1980s , and runs the Napanee count , as well as participating in other counts across the Kingston region every year . <p> " I 'm doing six or seven this year , and there are several other people who do that many , " Hennige said . " We enjoy being outside . " <p> The count is an annual compilation of bird species and their numbers in thousands of communities across North America . That data is gathered by volunteers -- there were 27 participants in Napanee , the highest number in years -- at bird feeders and out in the field between Dec. 14 and Jan. 4 . The tallies are then submitted to the National Audubon Society . <p> According to the National Audubon Society 's website , the 119th annual count saw 9,425 observers take part in 2,615 bird counts across the continent -- 460 of those counts taking place in Canada -- tally 48,678,334 birds total . <p> Jim Thompson , Chris Tsokos , and Kurt Hennige were three of 27 volunteers out counting birds in the Napanee region for the 120th annual Christmas Bird Count on Saturday , Dec. 22 , 2019 . They spotted some ravens and waterfowl at Finkle 's Shore Park in Bath before moving on to other areas on Saturday morning . Meghan Balogh/The Whig-Standard/Postmedia Networkjpg , KI <p> The number of birds counted has been dropping in recent years , and that can be due to many factors , including climate change , winter weather conditions , or the availability of local food . <p> Hennige said while this year 's counts in Napanee were low , especially at bird feeders , it was n't necessarily a bad sign . <p> " In general , birds do n't prefer feeder food . If they can get the natural food in the woods , they stay in the woods , " he explained . " The problem for many of the counts has been that the regular winter finches , redpolls , grosbeaks ( and more ) are n't showing up this winter . They 're staying 500 to 800 kilometres north of here in the Boreal Forest , because the Boreal Forest has one of the largest seed crops in many years . If you have food where you live in the summer , you stay there in the winter . " <p> Migrating is dangerous , Hennige pointed out . <p> " You migrate into different habitats , and do n't know where the food is or the predators are . If you do n't have to migrate , it 's a big benefit for the birds . " <p> Noting the yearly changes is what the Christmas Bird Count is all about . <p> " The point of the Christmas Bird Count is to get a good feeling of the common species , and where that population is . " <p> Hennige was impressed by the number of volunteers who were involved with the Napanee count this year . Twenty-seven individuals covered eight areas within the designated region from the north and east ends in Napanee and Newburgh , west to Deseronto and south from Sandhurst Shores to Bath . <p> " You could n't do citizen science like that without these people , " Hennige said . " They are going out , they 're embracing bad conditions , often cold temperatures . They are the stars of the Christmas Bird Count . They are really appreciated . " <p> To see this year 's bird count summary , which will be available sometime after Jan. 4 , 2020 , visit www.audubon.org. 
@@51297608 <h> Why UVic Faculty Massively Voted to Divest from Fossil Fuels <h> It 's time to walk the talk on reconciliation and the climate crisis . <p> James K. Rowe is an associate professor of environmental studies ; Lisa Chalykoff is an assistant teaching professor of English ; Jeff Corntassel ( Cherokee Nation ) is an associate professor of Indigenous Studies ; and Colin Goldblatt is an associate professor of Earth and ocean sciences . <p> Paarth Mittal is a student member of Divest UVic , a campus group that wants endowment and pension funds out of fossil fuel investments . Photo source : Divest UVic Facebook . <p> Last week a supermajority of faculty members at UVic ( 77 per cent ) voted in favour of fossil fuel divestment . Why ? Two of UVic 's major strategic priorities are " Promoting Sustainable Futures " and " Fostering Respect and Reconciliation . " These are values we pursue in our teaching , research and community engagement . For us , they are not buzzwords . <h> Announcements , Events &amp; more from Tyee and select partners <p> Our publication is stronger than ever , thanks to our amazing reader community . Now , can we stretch ? <p> Therefore , we think it is hypocritical for UVic to present itself as a sustainability and reconciliation leader while investing in companies that are primarily responsible for both the climate emergency and Indigenous dispossession . <p> For example , UVic has $2.5 million invested in Imperial Oil ( the Canadian subsidiary of ExxonMobil ) . Records show that Imperial Oil 's own scientists confirmed the realities of climate change as early as the 1970s , and yet the company has willfully pursued denial and policy obstructionism as an accumulation strategy . By investing millions of dollars into Imperial Oil , UVic is tacitly supporting its history of climate change denial ; indeed , the university is hoping to profit from it . That is sustainability leadership in high-speed reverse . <p> Many fossil fuel companies also contribute to the destruction of Indigenous lands and waters with their pursuit of new fossil fuel infrastructure projects . For example , UVic 's endowment fund has $700,000 invested in Teck Resources . Teck is currently pursuing one of the largest open-pit oil sands mines ever proposed . The project is in close proximity to many Cree and Dene families . According to Indigenous Climate Action , " This project threatens our Indigenous rights , ways of life , and ability to ensure the preservation of our lands and territories . " <p> The investment in Teck Resources contradicts UVic 's Strategic Plan and Indigenous Plan , which " commits to building and strengthening respectful relationships with Indigenous communities locally , provincially , nationally and around the world . " How can UVic claim that reconciliation and respectful Indigenous relationships are top priorities while materially investing in the ongoing dispossession of Indigenous peoples as well as destruction of their homelands and waterways ? <p> The moral case for divestment has always been strong but critics sometimes worry about the financial implications . Wo n't UVic 's endowment and pension funds lose money if they stop trying to profit from fossil fuel companies ? The answer is no . The financial case for divestment is growing stronger by the day . Remember that Imperial Oil investment ? It lost UVic over $700,000 last year . <p> Solar and wind stocks are outperforming oil and gas shares by a widening margin this year . Divested portfolios historically perform as well as , and often times better than , those invested in oil , gas and coal . Moreover , as energy generation shifts away from fossil fuels , investors who do not respond could be left with " stranded assets " -- investments that are no longer profitable . <p> ' Promoting Sustainable Futures ' and ' Fostering Respect and Reconciliation ' are stated major priorities for the University of Victoria . Aerial photo source : University of Victoria . <p> In the last four months alone , the University of California divested their $80-billion dollar portfolio , the European Investment Bank announced that it would stop lending to fossil fuel companies , and the Swedish Central Bank sold off its Alberta bonds because of that province 's high carbon footprint , which does not position the region well for the needed energy transition . More locally , UBC partially divested their endowment and their president has said that he 'd like complete divestment soon . UVic has lost its opportunity to lead -- but it is time we followed . <p> When we take on the fossil fuel industry , we take on one of the most politically and economically powerful industries in Canada . UVic researchers recently produced a report with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives showing how oil , gas , and coal companies are the biggest lobbyists in Canada . Indeed , over the last seven years the industry has averaged six lobby visits with the Canadian government per day for a total of over 11,000 visits . Likewise , the same people sitting on oil company boards are also on other boards , such as those that govern universities . The chair of UVic 's endowment fund , which is yet to divest , is also on the board of Horizon North Logistics which builds modular camps for oil sands production . <p> The votes of the majority of faculty at UVic last week signal that it is time for the university to walk its talk on sustainability and reconciliation and divest from fossil fuel companies . The young people at the heart of UVic 's mission deserve for our institutions to act honourably in solving the crisis that they will inherit . <p> Happy holidays , readers !
