@@51309803 <p> Members of a generation share a sense of history , a storyline on which they can place the present day . <p> Today 's stereotypical Boomer oldsters , for example , recall their generation 's victories over Communism , racism , sexism and homophobia , and imagine those oppressions are safely buried in the past . They see a modern world ordered by the rights and freedoms they fought to enshrine in law , from civil rights in America to Charter rights in Canada . They see this order threatened , however , by the doctrinaire overreach of the radicalized young , who have been ideologically trained not only to recognize old injustices , but to invent new ones , to lionize victims , and to parse the language of justice ever more finely until it vanishes into the dust of microaggressions , privilege , and pronouns that start with x . <p> This , at least , is Douglas Murray 's rough diagnosis in The Madness of Crowds , one of a recent spate of big idea books that sketch the contours of the generational culture wars , including also Meghan Daum 's The Problem With Everything and Robert Boyers ' The Tyranny of Virtue . <p> " Our public life is now dense with people desperate to man the barricades long after the revolution is over , " as Murray puts it in his description of how " legitimate human rights campaigns " in the last century such as feminism and racial equality went " through the crash barrier " and started demanding to be not just equal , but " better . " <p> " In each case a demonstration of virtue demands an overstating of the problem , which then causes an amplification of the problem , " Murray writes . <p> Got that , kids ? Everything is fine . <p> British author , journalist and political commentator Douglas Murray attends a photocall during the annual Edinburgh International Book Festival at Charlotte Square Gardens on August 13 , 2017 in Edinburgh , Scotland.Roberto Ricciuti/Getty Images <p> Describing generations is a bit like telling horoscopes . It is not science . It is impressionistic , subjective and context-dependent , like reading fortune cookies . But it can be weirdly convincing if you let it . Generations are more than just demographic cohorts . They are like signs of the Zodiac , each with a mood and a destiny that can only be fully divined if you suspend disbelief beyond all reason . When you do , though , familiar storylines fall into place , not only for history but for the future . <p> Gen Z youngsters see something different as they become adults in the Boomers ' retirement years . Stereotypical college kids today see high-principled laws that are skewed in practice against marginalized people . They see socioeconomic systems that perpetuate the same historical injustices their elders imagine have evaporated like a bad smell . They encounter resistance and condescension to their smallest efforts toward social justice , especially in the main Boomer blind spots of transgender and Indigenous rights . Their critical thinking is mocked as flighty indulgence , their newly coined words held up as evidence of cultish conformity in contrast to the Boomers ' plain spoken common sense and clear-eyed distaste for political correctness . Even the term " social justice " has been stolen and used to patronize these naive , brainwashed little " warriors . " <p> Ideologically , the generation gap has not seemed this wide since the 1960s , nearly a human lifespan ago , when the Boomers came of age with psychedelic fury and overthrew the stifling conformity of the retiring Greatest Generation , and not without a fight . <p> This dynamic is creating confusion and turbulence in diverse areas of the culture , from Hollywood to professional hockey , from campus politics to climate activism . Today , at the end of the twenty teens , the future is not what it used to be . <p> Signs are everywhere you look over the year just passed . Greta Thunberg , the teenage climate activist has become an improbable hero and an even less probable villain , and possibly the most generationally divisive character since U.S. President Donald Trump , who indulged in comically self-absorbed outrage when Time magazine named her Person of the Year . <p> Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg is pictured after disembarking from the catamaran La Vagabonde at the Santo Amaro docks in Lisbon , on December 3 , 2019 . CARLOS COSTA/AFP via Getty Images <p> At the other end of the age/gender/political spectrum there is Don Cherry , as timelessly familiar to Canadian Boomers as Mansbridge and Robertson , but curious to the young , like an old couch that is somehow still in the living room after a renovation . <p> Cherry 's firing and the cancellation of Coach 's Corner marked an important moment because it was one of the unusual instances of online outrage actually having a real world effect . His career was marked by frequent outrageous bigotry against French and European hockey players , but it finally collapsed because of a rant about immigrants he imagines not wearing the poppy . This was just Cherry being himself . It did not make a lot of sense unless you saw it through a generational lens . Then you realized you were looking at a racist dinosaur in a suit made of curtains , yammering through the intermission about some culture war talking point that has nothing to do with hockey . Then it became clear it was long past time for some new furniture . <p> Something is changing , in hockey as with the rest of the world . It was evident in the stories that came out after Mike Babcock was fired as coach of the Toronto Maple Leafs , especially from Chris Chelios , a defenceman who played for Babcock in Detroit . He had horror stories of vindictive spite , of the sort that would get you banned from beer league , let alone house league . He described Babcock " verbally assaulting " Johan Franzen on the bench , deliberately scratching Mike Modano at the end of his final season in 2011 to prevent him reaching 1,500 career games , and not letting Jason Spezza play a season opener this year against his former team , the Ottawa Senators . <p> It is one thing to mock a weak-kneed social justice warrior for saying words are violence and authority figures are too mean . It is different when it is Chelios , a three-time Stanley Cup champion . <p> This shift in the power of victimhood and outrage can be baffling to older observers . <p> Babcock is a rock-jawed leader from central casting , the cultural archetype of a boss , an alpha male who gets results and whose strategic use of cruelty might once have been excused , in the long run , on utilitarian grounds . It might even have been excused earlier this year , before the Maple Leafs embarked on a losing streak . <p> Former Toronto Maple Leaf Head Coach Mike Babcock scrums at Leaf year end availability in Toronto on Thursday April 25 , 2019 . Craig Robertson/Toronto Sun/Postmedia Network <p> But that line of thinking is lately showing its age . Young people have seen the power of speaking up and calling out . On their own they might seem like snowflakes . As a generation they can be a blizzard . <p> The flip side is evidenced in episodes like the recent Pocahontas scandal at Toronto 's Ryerson University , in which the student union president presided over a Social Justice Week workshop called Generations of Resistance , where an international student described as " Indigenous on her own land " sang " Colors of the Wind " from the Disney movie Pocahontas as a way to describe her own " personal resilience . " <p> Another student politician who is Indigenous said the song " triggered " her and could have been " traumatic " to others because it reminded her of another song in the movie , called " Savages . " As reported by The Eyeopener newspaper , the student union president pledged to vet musical performances at social justice workshops in future to prevent such cultural appropriation . <p> Taking critical thinking this far has bolstered the common view among Boomers that young people have been trained to seek out ever more subtle and complicated injustices , especially about representation and identity , and to invent them where they fail . <p> The result , typically , is a dead-end conversation in which hollow outrage is mansplained away , and no one learns anything except that the other side is deluded about the state of the world . They are not even thinking and arguing in the same way . <p> The young fetishize personal experience , which has left them vulnerable to ideological hucksters shopping diverse sob stories in the campus grievance industry and on the delusion amplifier of Twitter . But the old fetishize logic and supposedly unquestionable and timeless facts , which has left them vulnerable to deception on the post-truth internet . <p> Emotions set them apart too . If the young are drowning in performative empathy , the old are parched . This was illustrated in Nova Scotia recently , after a young alumna of St. Francis Xavier University took offence on Facebook that the new Brian Mulroney Institute of Government features a quote from the former prime minister 's father : " The only way out of a paper mill town is through a university door . " <p> " As a social worker in training , I need to speak out against oppression and discrimination , " Meaghan Marie Landry wrote in defence of the residents of mill towns , including herself , who should not be regarded as " impoverished and embarassing . " <p> Now , of course , this was widely mocked . Getting out of mill towns and fishing villages is what maritime life was all about in Mulroney 's childhood . It still is . That is literally Sonny 's Dream . But it was not just the young person who complained who got mocked . The university itself was harangued for apologizing . To the young , it looked like a school had humbly listened to criticism and apologized for inadvertently causing minor offence . To the old , it looked like an uppity scold on Facebook bullied the school 's president into submission and debasement , when he should have fought back . <p> In the National Post , columnist John Robson evoked imagery from Greek mythology and the French Revolution to suggest this Facebook post was like the story of Cronus ( the Roman god Saturn ) devouring his children for fear they were destined to overthrow him , as his sixth child Zeus eventually did . His point was that , in the famous words of the 18th century French anti-Revolutionary journalist Jacques Mallet du Pan , " Like Saturn , the Revolution devours its children . " Everything and everyone has become offensive in the " brave new ' how dare you ' world we have created , " Robson wrote . <p> In the cultural orbit of America , there has been a cataclysm once every lifetime , almost like clockwork <p> Compelling as the imagery was , Robson gave the game away by using the pronoun " we , " because of course sanctimonious indignation is not an invention of the young . People have been wondering how people dare forever . The English comedian Catherine Tate , for example , does a sketch character called Derek who is an older single man who lives with his mother and has a speaking manner that is gayer than Christmas . So when young people assume he is gay and treat him respectfully as such , his tagline , " How very dare you ! " is a caricature of a self-deluded Boomer whose crusty , outdated sense of place in the world has been challenged by a new morality of kindness and acceptance . <p> One thing you notice in these books about generational contrast is the frequency of insanity metaphors . There is plenty of religious and cultish language . Occasionally military images are called up for service . But it is the claims of insanity that stand out . <p> " How did our societies become so insane ? " lamented Eric Kaufmann , author of Whiteshift : Populism , Immigration and the Future of White Majorities in his Financial Times review of Murray 's book . <p> Kaufmann is a Canadian Gen Xer in his late 40s , but that is a question that would sound perfectly normal coming from the average Gen Z teenager of today , as he looks around at climate change , Brexit , Trumpism , and all the rest , and wonders how it got this way and what in hell the future might look like . <p> This sort of generational astrology has lately caught on , in part because it seems to be working better than ever . Traditional astrology has been packaged into memes and gifs as a Millennial trend of breezy self-care , so it is already current in popular culture . Intellectuals are at it too , both young and old , traditionalist and revolutionary . The theory of the Fourth Turning , a cyclical and quasi-mystical view of generation history that suggests we are now in the boundary years between the collapse of an old order and the rise of a new one , has taken on a sulphurous whiff of the dark arts through its endorsement by Steve Bannon , former Trump chief of staff and alt-right thought leader who is now rallying nationalist political groups in Europe . <p> Roughly , that theory observes that , in the cultural orbit of America , there has been a cataclysm once every lifetime , almost like clockwork . The American Revolution , Civil War , the Great Depression and World War II , and the 2008 financial collapse are all separated by about 80 or 90 years . All have led to the collapse of an old order and the rise of a new -- colony to republic , slavery to freedom , fascist threat to global hegemony . These periods are what the demographic economist Neil Howe calls Fourth Turnings , the final acts in four-part generational dramas in which the future seems uncertain , contingent , up for grabs . Things are changing and everyone knows it . This is what gives a Fourth Turning era its uneasy mood . The old order is dying and the new order is not yet born . <p> Things feel more apocalyptic today than they ever did for the Boomers , even with the threat of nuclear annihilation in their childhood , which they matured out of when they won the Cold War . The European security compact is falling apart , encouraged by a renegade American president . Centrist politics have weakened . The fringes are closing in . <p> It seems that way at least . Beliefs about the future are uncertain , not entirely rational . They resist argument . They involve fear and longing . They emerge from a shared story about the past . <p> So what we have in all this modern talk about how the young and old each regard the other as delusional lunatics are competing stories about how the past will determine the future , and what might be done to encourage or prevent that . These new books that sketch the battlefields of the culture war between old and young are not predictions , in the sense of rational arguments about what is likely to happen . They are horoscopes , readings of destiny in the stars . <p> A blood-soaked trail of interconnected traffickers and deals ran from the RCMP 's Operation Harrington to the Sinaloa Cartel <p> This Week 's Flyers <h> Comments <p> Postmedia is committed to maintaining a lively but civil forum for discussion and encourage all readers to share their views on our articles . @@51309812 <p> The history of humanity is a history of movement . Families , tribes , nations , armies , pilgrims , explorers , conquerors , liberators , traders , missionaries -- all on the move , along with their chattels and goods for trade , sometimes even their gods . <p> All that moving about , until the day before yesterday in historical terms , was thought to be a sign of progress . Citius , altius , fortius is the Olympic motto , but swifter , higher , stronger might well describe the history of transportation on our blue planet . And it was all judged to be better too -- the faster the better , the higher the better . <p> Not this year . Travel itself , especially by the progressive jet-set who travel most , was called into question as a measure of progress . Carbon emissions and so forth . <p> The history of humanity is a history of movement <p> Indeed , one of the big stories of 2019 was the enviro-pilgrimage of Greta Thunberg , the Swedish teenager who captured global attention with her apocalyptic climate activism . Thunberg , on her way to the holiest shrine of climate politics , a United Nations conference , decided to sail across the ocean to New York and back rather than fly . Fewer carbon emissions . <p> Modern travel has made pilgrimages easier -- pilgrims fly to Jerusalem , to Rome , to Mecca in hours where previously it had taken months on foot , by horse and camel and ship . Thunberg 's Atlantic sailing was a genuine hardship , like it was for the pilgrims of old . She spent 14 days at sea on the way over , sailing in a racing yacht with pails serving as bathroom facilities . On the way back it was 20 days in a 48-foot catamaran , facing 40-knot winds and five-metre high waves in a winter crossing . <p> Pilgrims travel to advance spiritually on the path to salvation . The Thunberg pilgrimage was for salvation of an earthly sort , to save the planet . <p> Sixteen-year-old climate activist Greta Thunberg sails into New York Harbor after a trans-Atlantic crossing to attend a UN summit on climate change , on Aug. 28 , 2019 . Mike Segar/Reuters <p> Christians lift their thoughts to salvation of a heavenly sort at Christmas . He shall be great , and shall be called the Son of the Highest : and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David . " <p> Gabriel was also sent to Zechariah , father of John the Baptist , in the Temple in Jerusalem . After receiving the news from Gabriel , Mary went " with haste " from Nazareth into the hill country of Judea , to the home of Zechariah and his wife , Elizabeth . Then it was back to Nazareth and later , with Joseph , the arduous trip to Bethlehem when she was great with child . After the birth , the Magi , the long-distance travellers from the east arrived . They departed , and Joseph , warned in a dream about the murderous plans of King Herod , fled with the mother and child into Egypt . They returned to Nazareth only after the wicked king was dead . <p> Pilgrims travel to advance spiritually on the path to salvation <p> The going down into Egypt and coming back to the land of Israel echoes the earlier great going-down and coming-up . The exodus of Moses and the children of Israel from Egypt was not only a journey of geography , but of history , politics and theology . A pilgrimage of salvation . <p> That is the heart of what Christians celebrate at Christmas , the great going-down of God . Jesus , as St. Paul tells us , " who , though he was in the form of God , did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped , but emptied himself , taking the form of a servant , being born in the likeness of men . " <p> And this great going-down of God , from heaven to Earth where " he pitched his tent among us , " is for a purpose , for the return journey . The learned theologians of the early Christian centuries were bold enough to say that " God became man so that man could become God . " A creature does not become his creator , so man does not become God , but he is offered the gift of God 's life share with him for all eternity . <p> A Christian pilgrim lights a candle on Christmas Eve as she visits the Church of the Nativity in the biblical West Bank city of Bethlehem on Dec. 24 , 2019 . Musa Al Shaer/AFP via Getty Images <p> The great going-down is so that there might be a great coming-up , but this time Jesus does n't return alone but with all those who are his disciples . That 's what Christmas means for Christians . <p> It is therefore a religion of progress , a story of a journey from worse to better , from slavery to freedom , conflict to comity , from transgression to redemption , from iniquity to holiness , from sin to mercy , from fallen nature to divinizing grace . Progress in the world , in earthly terms , often does not deliver on its promises , and sometimes is not even progress . The Christian idea of progress does not promise a better world , but that the world is now better . There was a before-Christ and an after , a great going-down so there can now be a great coming-up . <p> Here at the National Post we chronicle the comings and goings of the great and the powerful and the humble and the afflicted . Sometimes it is difficult to see progress in what we report about the world . Full Disclaimer <p> Erin Baerwald is a conservation biologist and assistant professor at the University of Northern British Columbia <p> As a bat biologist who has spent my entire 15-year career documenting and speaking out about the impact of wind turbines on bat populations , I never thought I 'd come out swinging in support of the wind-energy industry , but here I am . <p> The Dec. 4 decision by Ontario 's Environment Minister Jeff Yurek to cancel a 29-turbine wind farm that was under construction in Eastern Ontario is unwarranted and sets back bat conservation . <p> Story continues below advertisement <p> Mr. Yurek is clearly playing politics and did n't truly have bat concerns on his mind when he cancelled a project that had experienced earlier local opposition . <p> The minister justified the cancellation of this project by claiming it would -- in his view -- cause " serious and irreversible " harm to bat populations . His conclusion is in direct contrast to the finding of an environmental appeal tribunal , which found there was low risk to bat populations and that the mitigation measures adopted by EDP Renewables , the project developer , would further reduce the risk to bats , including species at risk . <p> Specifically , the tribunal found no evidence that the wind project would cause " serious and irreversible harm to plant life , animal life and the natural environment , " as laid out in Ontario 's Environmental Protection Act . <p> Mr. Yurek 's letter announcing the decision misrepresents the science by overstating the potential damage and misidentifying the species potentially harmed by the development . He 's not actually interested in reducing harm to bats . <p> Some wind farms deserve criticism for failing to mitigate impact on bats , but ignoring science and making false claims in order to shut down a site undermine legitimate efforts to protect bats . <p> Climate change is the biggest threat to biodiversity , including bats . Transitioning away from fossil fuels is critical in our fight against climate change . Wind energy is one of the cleanest forms of electricity production there is , but all forms of electricity generation have a cost . <p> It 's true that some wind projects can result in unacceptable levels of bat fatalities and that wind farms can harm bat populations , but it 's not every facility and it 's not every bat species . We have scientifically proven solutions to reduce , or even completely eliminate , bat fatalities . For example , we can reduce fatalities by as much as 50 per cent by shutting turbines off in low-wind speeds during bat migration , when most bats are killed . <p> Story continues below advertisement <p> EDP Renewables , which developed the Nation Rise site some 40 kilometres southeast of Ottawa , had voluntarily and proactively planned on implementing proven mitigation measures to reduce fatalities , which is something that other developers should emulate . The company did this in addition to actively trying to choose a site in a low-risk area for bats . I critically reviewed its impact assessment and it went above and beyond due diligence . Companies trying to do the right thing should not be penalized . This discourages other companies from taking on ambitious renewable energy projects , which sets back both bat conservation and our fight against climate change . <p> Bat populations are in trouble from a myriad of threats , but this scapegoating does not help them . In this case , it is clear that bats are being used to achieve other , more political objectives . If the minister were truly concerned about reducing bat fatalities , we could have achieved this in numerous ways that would have also allowed the turbines to generate carbon-free energy . <p> Bats should n't be used as political pawns . If the minster really cares about bats , he would find an avenue to fund research and conservation for their recovery , while helping us fight climate change -- one of the biggest challenges of our time . <p> Keep your Opinions sharp and informed . @@51311011 <p> As we come to the end of 2019 , it is time to review the year that was . It was in many ways a fairly tumultuous year in world affairs , but not greatly different from those that immediately preceded it . We continue to live in interesting , exciting and often depressing times . <p> The headlines were once again dominated by he who can truly be called the elephant in the room : Donald Trump . His ability to serially insult other leaders was once again much in evidence . His words served to undermine the solidarity of the Western alliance of nations . His kowtowing to dictators such as Russia 's Vladimir Putin and North Korea 's Kim Jong Un left a very bad taste in the mouths of many . His attempt to bribe the president of Ukraine into helping him demonize his Democratic opponent Joe Biden brought his office into disrepute and resulted in the House of Representatives impeaching him . While it is unlikely that the Republican-controlled Senate will vote to convict him , his presidency has already been badly tarred . It is very much to be hoped that he has been sufficiently damaged that American voters will show him the door in the 2020 presidential election . <p> The Brexit saga continued unabated throughout the year . When Prime Minister Theresa May resigned after having suffered three defeats in the House of Commons , she was succeeded by a mendacious populist in the form of Boris Johnson . He , too , went on to experience three parliamentary defeats , but he clung to power and called a general election . In a campaign notable for its nastiness and divisiveness , Johnson promised voters to " get Brexit done . " He also promised vast new investments in Britain 's struggling National Health Service and a variety of other social services . But as The Economist noted in a recent article , " Mr. Johnson is in many ways the ideal politician for a post-truth age , because nobody expects him to keep his word . He exists in a world of us-versus-them and of emotion rather than reason , a world in which cheering people up is more important than depressing them with facts . " That such a person could win a commanding majority in the House of Commons is a depressing commentary on the current state of British politics . <p> But beyond the politics of the Brexit debate , there are the policy issues which are all too often ignored in the heat of battle . Apart from wanting to leave the European Union , what do the Brexiters want for the country and the future ? There the answers are as muddled and confusing as the people putting them forward . As a commentator in the Globe and Mail noted following the announcement of the results of the election : " And so Britain is left with a driver very much in the driving seat , a powerful engine at his command , but also with no particular destination in mind . " This confusion will take a heavy toll on Britain 's future international relations and on its place in the world . It will also mean that " getting Brexit done " will hardly be the final chapter in this dismal episode in Britain 's history . We will no doubt be returning to it at the end of 2020 . <p> The election of President Emmanuel Macron had been widely hailed as bringing on to the world scene a true champion of a liberal democratic order . Macron has lived up to much of his promise , but has run into some serious head winds . Domestically , his government was confronted by the often-violent protests of the so-called " gilets jaunes " movement , which went on for months on end . Macron is now facing mass demonstrations by the country 's major labour unions , which are opposing his plans to reform France 's pension regime . In foreign policy , he set the cat among the pigeons with two remarks he made late in the year . The first was that NATO was " brain dead . " This was variously interpreted as a criticism of the United States and its failure to exercise leadership in the Alliance , and as yet another plug for his ambition to create a purely European defence alliance . His second remark was that the first priority of Western defence leaders should be terrorism rather than Russian adventurism . He even went so far as to suggest that the time had come for NATO to resume a political dialogue with the Kremlin . These ideas went over like the proverbial lead balloon with the Eastern European members of the Alliance . These comments , although disruptive , did have one redeeming result in the form of a decision by NATO to undertake an in-depth review of its strategy and purposes . <p> Unfortunately , populists continued to make headway in other parts of Europe in 2019 . Proponents of the Alternative for Germany achieved depressing results in a number of state elections . Populist parties continued to exercise power in Italy . And the populist governments in Poland and Hungary carried on with their programs of illiberal reform in the face of widespread public opposition . The governments of Italy , Poland and Hungary are testing the rules of the European Union more than they have ever been tested before . The European Union will be faced with many serious challenges in the year ahead , and Brexit will not necessarily be the most serious . <p> Beyond North America and Europe , the scene is , if anything , much darker . Bloody civil wars carried on unabated in Syria and Yemen , with catastrophic humanitarian results . The overthrow of two long-serving presidents in Algeria and Sudan has left these countries in a state of political chaos . Widespread political unrest is the order of the day in Iran and Iraq , and the efforts of their governments to maintain order have resulted in the deaths and wounding of thousands of people at the hands of security forces . The governments of Egypt and Saudi Arabia have continued to brutally repress and imprison all of their political opponents . And the latest pronouncements of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have made more remote than ever the prospects of a solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict . In short , in 2019 the Middle East remained one of the most cursed regions on earth . <p> The continent of Africa was only somewhat less grim . It nevertheless continued to experience a number of tragedies . The civil wars in the Democratic Republic of Congo , South Sudan and Somalia went on as before , claiming thousands of lives and creating intolerable situations for the civilian populations . Despite the best efforts of the United Nations , Mali remains the scene of Islamist extremist attacks and of more general ethnic rivalries . The extremists of Boko Haram and systemic mismanagement have contributed to making oil-rich Nigeria one of the saddest countries on the continent . And a combination of bad weather conditions and horrendous government has driven most of the population of Zimbabwe to the brink of starvation . And those same weather conditions are adversely affecting the populations of several countries in Southern and Eastern Africa . <p> There was also a bit of bad news emanating from Asia . There was no end in sight to the armed conflicts in Afghanistan . Pakistan was experiencing one of its frequent financial crises and was once again having to turn to the International Monetary Fund for a bailout . India 's Hindu Nationalist government carried on with its campaign to transform the country into a Hindu state as opposed to the secular state created by its founders . Its clearly anti-Muslim legislation on Kashmir and on citizenship has provoked widespread protests , many of which have turned violent . India 's 200 million Muslims now live in fear of what may come next . Myanmar 's Rohingya also live in terror as 700,000 of them experience yet another year as refugees living in makeshift camps in Bangladesh . The citizens of Hong Kong and the Uighurs of northwest China continue to experience repression at the hands of the Chinese government . <p> To counteract all of these dismal developments , there were a few good news stories in 2019 . The drawn-out negotiations of the new U.S. , Mexico and Canada trade agreement were finally brought to a successful conclusion and the agreement should be ratified in the new year . This outcome solidifies Chrystia Freeland 's status as Canada 's star cabinet minister . The end of the trial of SNC-Lavalin will allow the country to move forward from a particularly sad chapter in its political and economic history . What was perhaps the most exhilarating story of 2019 was the upsurge of young people around the world demanding action on climate change . Their forceful yet peaceful demonstrations gave the lie to the notion that the younger generation is apathetic . As exemplified by the young Swedish activist Greta Thunberg , they sent a powerful message to their elders that climate change had to be addressed urgently if the future of the planet is to be saved . Finally , at home there was the Liberal victory in the October general election and the subsequent demise of Conservative leader Andrew Scheer , both of which are good news stories in my book . <p> As I come to the end of this rather subjective review of 2019 , it remains only for me to wish you a happy and healthy New Year . <p> Louis A. Delvoie is a retired Canadian diplomat who served abroad as an ambassador and high commissioner . 
@@51311237 <p> There are some 37 million Canadians , and it would be unwieldy to ask each of them what they thought all the time ; in the same way , we ca n't sample each square inch of soil for nutrient level . <p> So we use statistical reasoning to sample just enough to grasp the larger picture . On a hundred acres if you randomly sample 10 or more spots , you will have a more than decent sample average . In statistics , it is generally accepted that sampling 100 individuals of any group will achieve the task at hand ; but more commonly , in assessing millions of people , a sample group of 1000 is used . <p> That is to avoid that one chance in 20 of missing the group altogether . <p> I am not here to talk about soil . <p> Any given week just in agriculture , the results of one poll or survey or another are released . It is a familiar tactic in the forever war of assessing or influencing public opinion . Sample one thousand people with questions and interpretations massaged enough to come up with the desired answer , and you can send a bill to someone . <p> One example this week is some poll or another about whether Canadians feel the food system is heading in the right direction . So 1000 clumps of soil -- I mean , Canadians -- had their moment in the sun to express an opinion about something they typically do n't think about , or could care less about unless it is just before lunch . <p> It is all nonsense , because no survey is ever publicized that delivers an answer the sponsoring organization is n't in favour of . <p> I used to wonder who pollsters were asking , because I can not remember ever being formally asked anything in my entire life . Can you ? <p> The answer to that lies in the numbers . <p> If there are 37 million Canadians then we should assume about 25 per cent of them are not able to be sampled -- too young or too old or living off the grid or under a rock . So let 's just say , if all samples are of 1000 people , on average we should expect as individual Canadians to be asked our opinion once in every 27,750 polls or surveys . <p> That seems remote , and it is . If we can estimate that there is at least a poll or survey a day in Canada , it turns out that we can expect as Canadians to be asked our opinion on something only once every 76 years . <p> If there are two surveys a day , or three , we maybe can look forward to being asked our opinion two or three times in a normal lifetime . These are still all trivial numbers . <p> I will be so annoyed if my lifetime moment comes and it is something like , do you think toilet paper should hang on the inside or the outside ? <p> It does n't matter though , because when my moment does come , I will likely do what I suspect so many Canadians do : refuse to be sampled . <p> Maybe my moment will come in a climate change survey , as there seem to be quite a few of these going on now . <p> Pollster : " Do you believe the earth is warming , that it is caused by humans , and placing us all in peril ? @@51311417 <h> ' Continue to be aspirational ' : Sudbury 's school of architecture plans to be around in 100 years <p> Officials from the McEwen School of Architecture updated city council on their progress earlier this month , taking time out to thank councillors for being an early supporter of the project . <p> The school opened in 2013 , led by founding director Terrance Galvin , and later opened a campus downtown , in the former location of the farmers market . <p> " We are here as a school and individuals because this council brought a bold vision of the school of architecture into downtown Sudbury -- from a far-fetched idea into reality when many doubted this could ever succeed , " said David Fortin , the current director of the school . <p> " When the first 70 students and six faculty arrived in Sudbury , we had no building or curriculum , but we were immediately immediately made to feel at home in this city . " <p> The school has now graduated its first class of architects , Fortin said , and now boasts 325 students , each paying $10,589 in tuition . When the 17-member faculty is included , as well as all their spending , the financial impact is more than $9.5 million a year in Greater Sudbury , he said . <p> And the first class of graduates " are now in the workplace , providing design leadership in Ontario and across the country , " Fortin said . " So on behalf of the students staff and faculty ... our first task tonight is to say thank you , merci and miigwetch to this council 's leadership foresight and continued support . " <p> The school has also achieved gender parity among its students , Fortin said , and students hail from six different countries . Most are still from Ontario , however , and half are from the North . <p> " We are the only school of architecture in the country to offer studios in both English and French , and the only one in the world who have elders and knowledge carriers present throughout the week as paid and valued contributors , " Fortin said . <p> While focused on Northern design and innovations , he said students still travel internationally to expand their outlooks and broaden their learning base . <p> " We want them learning from other places , and be inspired by them , " Fortin said . " Our study abroad opportunities have become an essential part of our student experience . But the core of our curriculum and our programs are the valued relationships with our communities and our aspiration to become the central design hub for Northern Ontario . " <p> Students have connected locally by taking part in different events , such as the Up Here festival and installations at the farmers market . Galvin , the school 's founding director , said they have a vision for the future -- a 20/20 vision for 2050 , to be exact . <p> That vision includes such things as the McEwen International Advisory Board , in which some big names in architecture can offer their input and guidance through public lectures and other special events . <p> " We made a conscious choice to be successful , and all of us -- faculty and students alike -- wish to take Sudbury to the next level over the next hundred years , " Galvin said . <p> " Part of our maturity is having a powerhouse McEwen International Advisory board that has our backs in terms of continuing to be innovative in architecture , both locally and globally . " <p> A design competition is also in the works , Galvin said , and could be focused on building carbon emission-free buildings for the future . In light of the city 's commitment to address climate change , the competition aims to elicit ideas on how to build with a much smaller carbon imprint . <p> " So the goal of the school , and the goal of the project , is to continue to be aspirational for Sudbury and to provide a visual language for ourselves , for the city and for the wider group of architects who are going to enter into the discussions with us , " he said . <p> " We hope that the competition will inform the updating and reframing of the ( carbon emissions ) master plan . @@51312921 <h> New industry develops around sucking carbon dioxide out of atmosphere <p> Somewhere in west Texas , amid one of the most productive oilfields in the continent , a Canadian company is building a plant that it hopes will eventually suck from the air a million tonnes of carbon being pumped out of the ground all around it . <p> Carbon Engineering 's groundbreaking plant is one of many projects hoping to help in the fight against climate change by turning its main driver -- carbon dioxide -- into a useful product that can be profitably removed from the atmosphere . <p> " We 're pulling the CO2 back down , " CEO Steve Oldham said in a recent interview . <p> People in labs and boardrooms around the world are beginning to confront the realization that more needs to be done than cut emissions if the world is to remain livable . Vast amounts of carbon already in the atmosphere will have to be removed . <p> A 2017 paper in the scientific journal Nature Climate Change calculated that to stabilize climate change at two degrees Celsius , between 120 billion and 160 billion tonnes of CO2 will have to be sucked from the air and stored underground . That 's in addition to Paris agreement emissions cuts . <p> That would cost big bucks . And that , says energy economist Mark Jaccard , is why companies such as Carbon Engineering are so important . Using CO2 to make marketable products will help pay for the massive scale-up of technology to remove CO2 and inject it permanently underground . <p> " You 're going to have to figure out some product you can make until humanity 's ready to use this for the real reason , which is to capture and bury carbon , " said Jaccard of the University of British Columbia . <p> Carbon Engineering is already pulling CO2 from the air and turning it into fuel at its pilot plant in Squamish , B.C. In Halifax , CarbonCure Technologies is injecting CO2 into concrete . <p> Many companies already inject CO2 underground to force more oil to the surface -- which , if done right , can result in carbon-negative oil . Other companies are using the gas to create useful chemicals , carbon nanotubes or plastics . <p> " There 's a number of technologies we 're trying to advance , " said Wes Jickling of the Canadian Oilsands Innovation Alliance . The group is helping run the Carbon XPrize , a $20-million award for the best conversion of CO2 into a saleable product . <p> The market for such products has been estimated at $1 trillion a year . <p> The question is whether that 's a prize adequate to drive innovation and construction fast enough to start reducing atmospheric CO2 before global temperatures rise past 1.5 degrees . That 's little more than a decade , according to the United Nation 's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change . <p> The technology for burying carbon underground , known as sequestration , is well understood and is being used at full-scale sites in Alberta and Saskatchewan . But in 2018 , the British Royal Society found that the pace of building such facilities needs to speed up by at least 100 times to meet the UN 's climate target . <p> Making products from CO2 also creates what 's known in climate circles as the moral hazard . If we can suck the gas out of the air , why bother emitting less of it ? <p> We ca n't count on a magic bullet to save us , said Jason Switzer , director of the Alberta Clean Technology Industry Alliance . <p> " There 's no question that we ca n't keep deferring hard choices , " he said . " We do have to make difficult choices . " <p> The world needs to emit far less carbon and take out much of what 's already there , Jaccard said . Building an industry based on removing it from the air is the best way to develop cheap and efficient ways of doing that . <p> " People have to figure how to get enough support for these technologies they know we 're going to need . @@51313739 <h> +24.32(+0.26%) <h> -1.36(-0.94%) <h> -3.10(-0.20%) <h> The Bedrock of Ultra-Low Yields Is at Risk <p> ( Bloomberg ) -- The new decade could be the dawn of a tougher era for bond investors , as conditions that sustained the historic bull run in government debt fall away . <p> Unprecedented central bank action has dominated economic stimulus since the global crisis and suppressed yields around the world . The skew may now be shifting more toward fiscal expansion that could pressure rates higher . Austerity is on the wane in Europe , spending packages are landing in Asia , and U.S. borrowing is on track for even bigger records in the next couple of years . <p> The handoff from monetary to fiscal policy is a longer-run investment theme , says Mark Dowding at BlueBay Asset Management , and he 's already trading it in the U.K. , by betting against gilts . <p> " When you look at the U.K. , what we 're witnessing now is some pretty material easing in fiscal policy , " said Dowding . " It 's a theme that we expect to see more broadly . " <p> The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development says government spending globally has helped widen the fiscal deficit from 2.9% of world gross domestic product in 2018 to an estimated 3.3% next year . Also , OECD economists are among the growing ranks pushing for more disbursements to tackle slowing global growth and climate change . <p> The trouble for investors is working out when government spending may reach a critical mass to push yields higher . As of now it 's still in fledgling stages , while central banks continue to pump massive stimulus . <p> " To me this is the story of the next decade , " said Elaine Stokes , portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles &amp; Co . " The green shoots of fiscal spending are happening across the globe , but it has n't gotten to a place where it is coordinated . " <p> " In the next 5 to 10 years it becomes a factor in markets , " Stokes said . " So that 's where the market has to go -- we have to turn to a rising rate environment from a falling rate environment . " <p> From South Korea to Brazil , a Global Guide to Stimulus Plans in 2020 <p> The risk of a reversal in the last decade 's trend of falling yields is palpable . The governments of the two largest economies are spending more , and relying on debt to plug much of their revenue shortfall . Alicia Garcia-Herrero , chief economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis SA , sees China 's issuance growing as the budget gap widens from 7.9% this year to 9% of GDP . <p> " Monetary policy has been less effective by itself , especially in the EU and China , the economy thus calls for more expansionary fiscal policy to grow , " said Garcia-Herrero , who previously worked for the European Central Bank and the International Monetary Fund . " One drawback of fiscal expansion is its upward pressure on interest rates . " <p> So far that pressure is barely registering in borrowing costs . The world 's benchmark , the U.S. 10-year yield , is mired below 2% , and $11 trillion of debt worldwide yields less than zero . While that total has shrunk by more than a third since August -- when global yields troughed -- investors continue to seize on assets that offer some return . And it still looks way riskier to trade against haven flows and central bank purchases while the global economic outlook remains fragile . <p> That 's a popular and persuasive case against higher yields in the U.S. for now , even as lawmakers on both sides of the aisle look ready to embrace blowout deficits . The Treasury may manage to keep borrowing steady this year -- albeit at a record level -- in part because the Federal Reserve 's current plan to stabilize short-term funding rates could trawl roughly $240 billion of bills out of the market in the coming months . <p> Investors like Dowding are focusing on regions where monetary policy looks most exhausted . He reckons the market is overestimating the likely stimulus from the Bank of England . And his call in the U.K. is n't an outlier -- Goldman Sachs Group Inc. strategist George Cole estimated that issuance to fund current spending and public-sector investment could be worth a boost of around 25-40 basis points in gilt yields next year . <p> Across the channel , ECB President Christine Lagarde is clearly taking up the push for more fiscal spending and may have more success than her predecessor . That said , expansive policy is emerging mainly in the peripheral countries , as a backlash against austerity . The region 's savers -- including its largest economy -- are n't showing much sign of shifting their stance . <p> " We 've seen this movie before , " said Brad Setser , senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations . " There is building pressure in Germany to increase investment and increase green investment in particular , but so far it has n't catalyzed an enormous shift in policy . " <p> Lagarde Eyes Dozen Euro Members With Precious Room to Spend More <p> In Japan , BNP Paribas SA sees increased government spending helping the 10-year yield edge up to +0.1% in 2020 from its current level just below zero . <p> But the Bank of Japan is scooping up bonds at such a rate , it 's still swamping fiscal efforts so far , according to UBS chief Japan economist Masamichi Adachi . This month 's $239 billion spending package may be only just enough to avert a recession following October 's sales-tax increase . <p> " The stimulus package is n't a bold shift from the past and wo n't significantly affect the outlook for markets or the Japanese economy , " Adachi said . " At most , it helps support confidence . " <p> But the rationale for higher yields is in place , at least in theory . S&amp;P Global Ratings ' leading arbiter on the quality of the world 's government debt said that it 's gotten sketchier , as countries have seized on low interest rates to borrow more . <p> " You 're looking at close to 65 or 70% of world GDP that has today a lower credit quality than it had pre-2008 crisis , " said Roberto Sifon Arevalo . Government debt is " riskier today than it was before , but it 's not reflected in the market . " <p> Emerging markets have tended to pay a higher price for profligacy than developed economies with more room to spend , he said . And it 's worth remembering that when S&amp;P cut the U.S. 's top-shelf credit rating , in 2011 , Treasury yields plummeted as investors flooded into the world 's safest debt market . But the overall trend is clear . <p> " The market seems a bit complacent with the idea that interest rates will stay low for the foreseeable future , " said Sifon Arevalo . <p> To contact the reporters on this story : Emily Barrett in New York at ebarrett25@bloomberg.net ; Chikako Mogi in Tokyo at cmogi@bloomberg.net ; James Hirai in London at jhirai3@bloomberg.net <p> To contact the editors responsible for this story : Benjamin Purvis at bpurvis@bloomberg.net , Debarati Roy 
@@51314107 <p> In June , Olga Comeau and other Extinction Rebellion members barricaded a logging road near Corbett Lake in an effort to halt cutting in an old biodiverse forest on Crown land . - Lawrence Powell <p> In 2020 , and the decade it ushers in , expect the pointy end of the spear to pierce the old , entrenched economic order with increasing frequency . <p> Extinction Rebellion 's Nina Newington used the " pointy end of the spear " analogy to define a citizens ' group that banded together , got some expert help , and saved -- at least for now -- an Annapolis County forest slated for harvest last summer . <p> The citizens ' group coalesced after Round Hill 's Bev Wigney decided to try to save the mature forest that stands between Dalhousie and Corbett lakes in Annapolis County some 10 kilometres south of Bridgetown . <p> An essential assist came in June from naturalist Scott Leslie , whose discovery of a magnolia warbler in the forest led to a temporary halt in the harvest . Under the federal Migratory Birds Convention Act , the warbler ca n't be disturbed during its nesting season , and Leslie got GPS co-ordinates and photographs show the bird nesting . <p> Lands and Forestry Minister Iain Rankin called the halt but his intervention , after Leslie 's discovery , tells us a couple of things . First , do n't count on the province to identify habitat that 's supposed to be protected . And second , environmental advocates need to know the laws so they can use them to their advantage , and , for that , they may need some expert advice . <p> Citizens groups coming together to protect the natural environment are becoming increasingly common . They may be " the pointy end of the spear , " but growing environmental awareness and concern for its protection are resulting in more force -- and political clout -- behind the spear 's tip . <p> The Friends of the Northumberland Strait took up the fishermen 's opposition to Northern Pulp 's plan to deposit treated pulp mill effluent in the Strait . A group called Sustainable Northern Nova Scotia coalesced around opposition to gold mining in the Cobequid Hills . And on the province 's Eastern Shore a growing number of citizens are coming together in opposition to gold mines planned in their region . <p> For years , governments in Nova Scotia and elsewhere have been telling citizens that they 'll strike a balance between the economy and the environment . But , until recently , the economy out-weighed the environment every time . <p> When Premier McNeil stuck to his guns to close Boat Harbour on schedule , effectively shutting down Northern Pulp because the mill had no approved way to treat its effluent , it signalled that , at least in that case , the environment had a fighting chance . <p> In November , East Coast Environmental Law put on a seminar to help people understand the essentials of environmental law in Canada and in Nova Scotia and identify how the laws can help their efforts to protect the environment . <p> Eastern Shore residents , concerned about more open pit gold mines planned for their region , were well represented among a few dozen souls who attended that session . <p> Most of those folks never dreamed of becoming environmental activists , but now they represent the pointy end of the spear that will try to pierce plans for more gold mines on the Eastern Shore and near the St. Mary 's River . The Moose River mine in Halifax County is Nova Scotia 's only working gold mine . <p> Groups like Extinction Rebellion have adopted a disruptive approach to stop environmental damage because , faced with both a species extinction and climate crisis , they say official action is n't coming fast enough . <p> Heightened environmental anxiety , driven mostly by climate change , is elevating the environment on the list of public concerns , and closing the gap between the environment and the economy . <p> Activists and ad hoc citizens groups may be the pointy end of the spear but growing public sympathy for the causes they champion is putting politically potent force behind that spear . <p> Do n't expect governments to lead the charge to protect the environment at the risk of economic activity . After all , a growing economy feeds government coffers and gives them the cash they need to do the things that traditionally get them re-elected . <p> But it 's hard to parry the tip of the spear when it comes with the force of a motivated public behind it . That spear can pierce the entrenched economic interests that have called the shots for a long time but , in the coming years , will have to learn environmentally responsible practices or pack their bags and leave , at the pointy end of a spear . <p> Jim Vibert , a journalist and writer for longer than he cares to admit , consulted or worked for five Nova Scotia governments . He now keeps a close and critical eye on those in power . 
@@51314407 <h> +28.08(+0.30%) <h> -1.35(-0.93%) <h> -3.10(-0.20%) <h> New Brunswick premier hopeful for development of small nuclear reactors <p> FREDERICTON -- The premier of New Brunswick says the development of small nuclear reactors may be the answer to the economic and clean-energy needs of the province . <p> In a year-end interview with The Canadian Press , Blaine Higgs says the small modular reactors being developed in New Brunswick will be able to provide energy while addressing climate change the massive amount of energy that is needed , with zero emissions , " he said . <p> Earlier this month , New Brunswick signed a memorandum of understanding with Ontario and Saskatchewan to collaborate on the development of small modular reactors ( SMRs ) . <p> Two companies , ARC Nuclear Canada and Moltex Energy , have both set up offices in New Brunswick to develop prototypes . Each has committed $5 million to operations and research . <p> " The SMR technology is very different than the traditional Candu technology , " Higgs said , referring to the Canadian-invented deuterium uranium technology used in reactors in Point Lepreau , N.B. , and elsewhere . <p> " Both technologies use a fraction of uranium that is used in the Candu reactors . " <p> Last year , the New Brunswick government announced a commitment of $10 million towards nuclear research . <p> The premier said he also wants to push for more exploration of natural gas in the province . <p> " Yes , we may be moving away from some of the traditional fossil fuels , but there is a process , " he said . <p> " There is a process moving from oil to gas and gas to nuclear , and then solar and wind . That 's what we have to get in acceptance here in this province because we 've got it right under our nose , and we sit around and say no . " <p> In June , Higgs ' Progressive Conservative government quietly passed regulatory changes that would allow the extraction of hydrocarbons through the process known as fracking , in the Sussex area . <p> The move fulfilled a commitment in the government 's throne speech and was consistent with the Tories ' past support for fracking . <p> Mi'kmaq and Wolastoqey leaders denounced it as secretive and a step backwards in the province 's relationship with Indigenous populations . <p> This report by The Canadian Press was first published on Dec. 30 , 2019. 
@@51314648 <h> Social Sharing <h> Magnitude of situation facing huge numbers of world 's children in 2020 is ' heartbreaking ' <p> Children stand next to a metal barrier as newly arrived refugees and migrants wait to be registered at the Moria camp on the island of Lesbos , Greece , on Nov. 27 . ( Elias Marcou/Reuters ) <p> This column is an opinion by David Morley , president and CEO of UNICEF Canada . For more information about CBC 's Opinion section , please see the FAQ . <p> We are entering the final year of what has been one of the worst decades for children . War , disease and extreme weather events are robbing them of their right to simply be a kid -- to have a safe , healthy and carefree childhood . <p> In far too many communities around the world , sounds of youngsters laughing and getting into mischief are being replaced by silence . It does n't have to be that way . <p> This month , UNICEF launched Humanitarian Action for Children 2020 , a report on the world 's emergencies . It highlights some of the key challenges children are facing around the world : severe malnutrition , conflict , infectious disease , climate change , and access to education . <p> Children displaced by crises are also vulnerable to increased harm , including gender-based violence , recruitment as soldiers , exploitation , and trafficking . <p> A boy holds a rifle as he attends a rally of Houthi movement supporters to mark the Ashura in Sanaa , Yemen , on Sept. 10 . ( Khaled Abdullah/Reuters ) <p> The sheer magnitude of the situation is heartbreaking . <p> The report identifies 59 million children in 64 countries who are living in crisis zones and in need of urgent humanitarian assistance , including 2 million children with disabilities . These are the highest levels since we began keeping records . <p> The projections for the year ahead are just as dire . <p> The main causes are threefold -- conflict , climate change and major outbreaks of disease . <h> Conflict <p> The number of armed conflicts is at a three-decade high , with many civil wars engulfing entire countries . <p> Fighting has been going on for six years in both the Central African Republic and South Sudan . <p> Syria 's civil war is now in its ninth year . <p> And these conflicts have no end in sight . Some have lasted so long that many kids are growing up only knowing war . <p> Displaced Yemeni seven-month-old baby Mohammed Hussein , suffering from malnutrition , is brought by his mother to be checked at a hospital in Yemen 's conflict-ridden northwestern Hajjah governorate . ( Essa Ahmed/AFP/Getty Images ) <p> Top priorities in these war-torn regions include providing children with protection , safe water and sanitation , health care and nutrition . And the need is great . <p> In the coming year , for example , UNICEF expects it will need to treat 5.1 million children for acute malnutrition , provide 4.5 million children and caregivers with mental health and psychosocial support , and distribute emergency cash assistance to 1.7 million families to meet their most urgent needs . <h> Education <p> Immediate responses to crises in the year ahead must also be balanced with the longer-term needs of children , most importantly their education , which is also under attack . <p> During disasters , schools are often used as shelters or distribution centres , since they are usually among the strongest structures . <p> In conflict zones , they are increasingly becoming targets . <p> Afghan schoolchildren study at the destroyed Papen High School in Deh Bala district of Nangarhar province in July . ( Noorullah Shirzada/AFP via Getty Images ) <p> More than 3,000 schools have been closed in Burkina Faso , Mali and Niger in the past three years because of violence and insecurity . <p> Kids are incredibly adaptable , but in any emergency , getting them back into a classroom as quickly as possible is essential . Education to help them reach their potential is obviously important , but letting them be with their friends in a safe space also gives them a return to normalcy . <h> Disease <p> As if wars and conflict were n't enough , millions of children are also threatened by outbreaks of highly contagious and dangerous diseases . <p> Major outbreaks are now hitting the most vulnerable in conflict zones , greatly complicating the ability of aid agencies to respond . <p> A Ugandan health worker administers Ebola vaccine to a child in Kirembo village , near the border with the Democratic Republic of Congo in the Kasese district of Uganda , in June . ( James Akena/Reuters ) <p> The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is the second-largest ever recorded and the first to occur in the middle of a conflict zone . There are 3,000 confirmed cases , including more than 900 children . <p> Measles has also become a threat to children despite safe and affordable vaccines . As with any public health campaign for children , educating the adult decision-makers is the key to eliminating this deadly threat . <h> Climate <p> Climate change is also affecting the most vulnerable . <p> More than 500 million children live in areas that have experienced extreme flooding , while 160 million live in regions that are subject to severe drought . <p> And the number of extreme weather events keeps rising . Mozambique was hit by back-to-back cyclones earlier this year , for example , and rebuilding will take years . <p> Children help clean the makeshift migrant camp after major rainfall hit the island of Chios on Dec. 11 , where thousands of refugees and migrants live in squalid conditions without water and electricity . According to government figures , hundreds more are arriving daily . ( Louisa Gouliamaki/AFP via Getty Images ) <p> Regions like the Sahel in Africa , where livelihoods rely on agriculture , grazing and fishing , are especially susceptible to the effects of climate change . <p> Solutions demand a long-term commitment . The positive news is that humanitarian organizations have made tremendous progress working with host governments in areas likely to experience extreme weather and flooding , helping to build more resilient communities and better prepare for disasters . <p> Still , the threats children are facing are overwhelming . The amount of funding for emergencies that UNICEF projects it will need in 2020 is $4.2 billion US , a staggering 3.5 times the amount required in 2010 , underscoring how frightening the world has become for young people . <p> But as someone who has worked in the international humanitarian sector for going on four decades , I refuse to be discouraged . We can not give up . <p> The international community , governments and civil society need to come together to protect and defend children 's rights . <p> The government of Canada is playing a global leadership role in prioritizing education for children in conflict zones and other protracted humanitarian crises . But as a nation we must do more to help children around the world . <p> People in this country clearly care about children 's welfare . I am confident Canadians will rise to the challenge and defend , for every child everywhere , the right to a safe and healthy childhood . <p> This column is part of CBC 's Opinion section . For more information about this section , please read our FAQ . <h> Related Stories <h> Comments <p> To encourage thoughtful and respectful conversations , first and last names will appear with each submission to CBC/Radio-Canada 's online communities ( except in children and youth-oriented communities ) . @@51314649 <h> Social Sharing <h> On P.E.I. , a ' different breed ' of conservative government -- are they ' green Tories ? ' <p> While conservative governments in Alberta and Ontario resist definitive action to reduce emissions and the federal Conservatives seek new leadership and direction , P.E.I. 's new PC government offers an alternative approach . <h> Social Sharing <h> As conservatives across the country resist efforts to reduce emissions , Island PCs chart a different course <p> Prime Minister Justin Trudeau meets P.E.I. Premier Dennis King in his Parliament Hill office on Nov. 7 . Under King , the Progressive Conservatives have set a long-term emissions target similar to Trudeau 's target for the rest of the country -- to be carbon neutral by 2050 . ( Adrian Wyld/Canadian Press ) <p> In Alberta in 2019 , the new United Conservative government under Jason Kenney created a $30-million " energy war room " to battle the environmental movement . <p> In Ontario , Progressive Conservative Premier Doug Ford said he was " proud " to tear up hundreds of green energy contracts after coming to power , at an estimated cost to provincial taxpayers of $230 million . <p> And while those two provinces and Saskatchewan continue to challenge the federal carbon tax in court , another conservative provincial government is headed in a completely different direction when it comes to climate change and the environment . <p> Dennis King led the Progressive Conservatives back to power in Prince Edward Island in 2019 after 12 years in opposition . Leading a minority government with the Greens as the Official Opposition , King has called climate change " the seminal issue of our time . " <p> " I believe that as a responsible citizen we have to be concerned about our environment , " said King " We have to work to chart a different course . Does that make me a ' green Tory ' or whatever the label could be ? I do n't know . " <h> P.E.I. 's green shift <p> As the term ' red Tory ' has come to define conservative politicians who champion socially progressive policies , consider the growing evidence of ' green Toryism ' in P.E.I. : <p> In mandate letters , King instructed all his cabinet ministers to consider the climate impact of their portfolios , while his government created climate change co-ordinators to find ways to reduce government emissions in each department . <p> While most of his caucus voted against it , King himself supported legislation put forward by the opposition Greens to set a more ambitious 2030 emissions target for P.E.I. That bill passed with support from the third-party Liberals . <p> When the King government 's first throne speech included a mention of its new " long-term vision " to make P.E.I. carbon neutral , the Greens pushed until King put a date on that vision -- 2050 , the same year the Trudeau Liberals have set as the target to bring the rest of the country to net-zero emissions . <p> Something 's happening on Prince Edward Island -- and it 's pretty amazing ! Not only are they building sustainable communities , but they 're also aiming to be net-zero within 15 years . Plus , because it affects everyone , all parties are working together to tackle climate change . &lt;a href= " https : //t.co/4AuWkzloMK " &gt;pic.twitter ... Long tradition of environmental conservatives , says former minister <p> Tom McMillan , a former P.E.I. MP who served as environment minister under Brian Mulroney , said there 's nothing new in a conservative administration in Canada championing the environment . <p> " There is a tradition of concern for the environment in the party , it 's just that it had lost its way with Stephen Harper and the Harperites and now with certain provincial governments , notably Alberta and ... in the Ford administration in Ontario , " said McMillan . <p> McMillan was environment minister when the Mulroney government helped broker a multilateral deal to restrict the use of ozone-depleting chlorofluorocarbons ( CFCs ) . <p> He said it makes practical and political sense for the Island PCs to show what he described as a " green ethos , " and that in doing so they 're being true " to their very nature as Islanders . " <p> Alberta Premier Jason Kenney , left , met P.E.I. Premier Dennis King soon after King was elected . King has made it clear he 's not joining the so-called conservative " resistance " movement in Canadian politics . ( Steve Bruce/CBC ) <p> " It 's in our DNA to be environmentalists , " McMillan said of Islanders ' reliance on the environment to support their three primary industries of fishing , farming and tourism . <p> " The Island is more vulnerable to climate change than any other part of Canada . That 's just a fact . We are a low-lying sandbar in the North Atlantic . " <h> Time for Conservatives to take climate change seriously , says King <p> King said as a PC , there 's no " natural home " for him on the federal political stage and he no longer carries a membership in the Conservative Party of Canada . <p> He said it is time for other conservatives -- particularly the federal party , now that it 's in search of a new leader -- to take environmental issues more seriously . <p> " I am a Progressive Conservative . I 'm very much aware coming from an island province what the environment and the changing environment mean . <p> " I just think that the electorate nationwide is much more astute and into those ideas than what perhaps the federal party has paid enough attention to . " <h> Talk is cheap , say Greens ... <p> King says there 's no question the rise of the Green Party on P.E.I. , from a lone member in 2015 to Official Opposition four years later , has shaped Island politics and his own view on environmental issues . <p> But Green Leader Peter Bevan-Baker is n't ready to affix the term " green " to the PCs just yet . <p> P.E.I. 's Opposition leader Peter Bevan-Baker , right , and Premier Dennis King have become known for their cordial working relationship and for sharing the occasional hug . Both say the rise of the Green Party has shifted Island politics . ( CBC ) <p> " I think that it is a different brand , a different breed of Tory government that we have here on Prince Edward Island . I do n't know if I 'd go as far to call them ' green Tories ' , " said Bevan-Baker . <p> He points to the PCs continuing with the carbon tax plan laid out by the previous P.E.I. Liberals , which has the province reducing its provincial gas tax to offset increases in the carbon tax . Bevan-Baker and other critics have said that makes the carbon tax useless as a tool to reduce emissions . <p> " The Tories are pretty good at talking a good game on climate change , but words , as they say , are cheap , " said Bevan-Baker . <p> But he said the Island PCs are a reflection of the changing priorities of Island voters , who themselves , he says , reflect a shift happening around the world . <p> " I think the public is already there , saying we need to do better , we have to be serious " about the climate crisis , he said . <p> What the Tories under King have realized , he suggested , is " that perhaps the political peril associated with being bold on this climate crisis is not a political impediment at all . In fact it 's something that most Islanders will be cheering them on for . " <h> Comments <p> To encourage thoughtful and respectful conversations , first and last names will appear with each submission to CBC/Radio-Canada 's online communities ( except in children and youth-oriented communities ) . But the reality is that on environmental and energy issues , the government remains on the same path of disruption and destruction that defined its first piece of legislation that dismantled the previous government 's climate change strategy . <p> Rather than changing direction in response to the auditor 's report , the government 's assault on the environment seems to be continuing . Its most recent iteration is Bill 132 , a massive omnibus bill ostensibly aimed at reducing " red tape " adopted last week . Buried in its details is an attempt to undo the previous Liberal government 's moratorium on neonicotinoid pesticides , widely identified as posing serious risks to pollinators . <p> Other provisions of the act weakened the rules around forestry operations , mining , water taking , gravel pits and quarries and pollution . <p> The government is moving forward with a parallel proposal that would dismantle the province 's regulatory framework for controlling industrial water pollution , first established in the early 1990s as the Municipal-Industrial Strategy for Abatement ( MISA ) program . <p> The province is proposing to move away from the MISA program 's province-wide pollution limits for each major industrial sector and return to the pre-MISA model of negotiating pollution limits on a facility-by-facility basis . The underlying goal seems to be to make it easier to authorize increased discharges of both conventional and toxic water pollutants . <p> The MISA rules are now 25 years old , and there have been calls from the former environmental commissioner 's office and others for their overhaul and updating . Instead , the Ford government is effectively proposing to turn the clock back on how the province manages industrial water pollution to more than half a century ago . <p> The ongoing tragedy of mercury poisoning at Grassy Narrows from a pulp mill that operated at Dryden , Ont. in the 1960s and 1970s speaks to the effectiveness of that kind of regime . <p> The Ford government seems to have missed the point of the October federal election . The inability of the federal Conservatives to articulate an effective strategy to deal with climate change was one of the reasons they failed to make any electoral inroads in Ontario . <h> YOU MIGHT BE INTERESTED IN ... <p> Where the government goes from here is an open question , but there is an old saying that if you find yourself at the bottom of a hole , the first thing you do is to stop digging . <p> For the Ford government on the environment , good places to stop digging would be to end its quixotic crusade against carbon pricing , reconsider implementation of the retrograde measures in Bill 132 and halt the effort to dismantle the MISA program .
